Convex regression encompasses a wide array of methodologies utilized across numerous fields, including production, finance, and machine learning. This research introduces pyStoNED, a flexible and extensible Python library designed for convex regression and frontier estimation. pyStoNED offers a unified interface that accommodates diverse data configurations and regression models, supporting both single and multi-output scenarios. The toolkit employs a modular architecture to facilitate easy access to model specifications, data handling, and visualization tools. By leveraging convex optimization, the package ensures robust and reliable results. The authors demonstrate the utility of pyStoNED through various empirical examples and provide an overview of its internal structure.

We present a detailed examination of the LHC's potential to detect the SM-like Higgs boson ($\phi$) in the $t \bar t \phi$ decay channel, which is the most promising scenario for a heavy top partner. This process is characterized by a substantial cross section and a unique kinematic profile, where the Higgs boson is notably energetic and the top quarks are often off-shell. We assess the LHC's discovery reach for this signature, incorporating the latest advancements in both detector capabilities and top parton phenomenology. Our analysis reveals that the $\sigma \times \epsilon$ sensitivity for this channel is competitive with other production modes, particularly in the high-mass region where the Higgs boson exceeds 600 GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this signature is highly robust against uncertainties in the background, even when accounting for uncertainties in top parton production cross sections.

We introduce a straightforward technique for extracting few-shot and unsupervised task-related information from pretrained language models. This method involves generating numerous diverse sentence pairs using the model, calculating their similarity scores, and filtering for those that exhibit both high individual similarity and high variance across them. We demonstrate the utility of this selected data for training task-specific models, creating dense embeddings via contrastive loss, and facilitating human analysis of model behaviors. Furthermore, we show that these sentence pairs can serve as a self-supervised anchor to align a model's internal representations with human semantic understanding.

This study introduces an open-source, automated speech recognition system for German, built using deep neural networks. We detail the integration of various data sources and the development of a comprehensive German speech database. Additionally, the paper evaluates different training strategies and decoders, ultimately proposing the German Grapheme-Phoneme model. The resulting system achieves a Word Error Rate of 22.2% on the AIShell-Speech development set. All resources and code are hosted publicly at https://github.com/MichaelFritzen/german-asr.

This study presents a comprehensive investigation of 30 candidate Be stars within the 30 Doradus region, utilizing 30 spectra obtained via the VLT/FORS2 instrument. The analysis covers their spectral characteristics, variability, and physical properties. We identified 13 confirmed Be stars, 11 likely Be stars, and 6 non-Be stars. Among the 13 confirmed Be stars, 11 are located in the core of 30 Doradus, while 2 are in the periphery; notably, 10 of the latter reside in HII regions, and 1 is situated in a star cluster. These 13 Be stars span a wide range of spectral subtypes, from B0 to B9.5. Based on our analysis, the majority exhibit characteristics consistent with classical Be stars, whereas the remaining two display traits aligning with high-excitation line (HEL) objects. Furthermore, we observed that the majority of these stars show spectral variability, with 10 of them showing changes in their emission lines.

Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) converts spoken language from normalized forms into written text. While recent research has applied data-driven approaches to ITN, achieving the best results typically requires vast amounts of training data. This paper introduces a novel data augmentation technique designed to bolster existing datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark corpus, specifically requiring only a minimal increase in dataset size to yield these gains.

This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermitian operator subject to Robin boundary conditions on a smooth strictly convex hypersurface $\Sigma$ within $\mathbb{R}^n$. Additionally, we derive a corresponding inequality for the Hermitian operator under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, respectively.

Kernel methods are a powerful class of algorithms that map data into high-dimensional feature spaces to identify complex patterns. A critical factor in this process is the kernel function, which quantifies the similarity between data points. While most existing kernels are designed to operate on exchangeable data—where data points are drawn independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.)—this assumption fails for data exhibiting local structures, such as graphs or manifolds. To address this, we introduce non-exchangeable kernels capable of incorporating data-specific adjacency information. We provide a rigorous theoretical framework for these kernels, demonstrating their ability to capture intricate local patterns. Furthermore, we develop an efficient sampling strategy that ensures computational scalability. Empirical results across various tasks confirm that our kernels outperform traditional approaches in handling non-i.i.d. data.

Non-Hermitian systems exhibit unique topological classifications, including point-gap topology. While correlations are generally thought to disrupt non-trivial topology in Hermitian systems, we demonstrate that they can similarly reduce the topological index associated with the first homotopy group of the energy's point-gap structure. Specifically, we investigate an interacting 1D non-Hermitian model featuring open boundary conditions, where interactions are mediated by correlated hopping. We find that correlation-induced shifts in the ground state can lower this topological index. Remarkably, we also identify a non-trivial topological phase that persists even when the ground state is uncorrelated, provided the excited states retain correlations. These findings establish point-gap topology as a distinct entity from many-body ground state properties.

This study examines the inclusion of social traits—such as speaker age and sociolinguistic variables like social class and style—within synthetic speech. We evaluate multiple modeling strategies for encoding these traits and introduce a novel Variational Autoencoder-based Variational Acoustic Model (VAM) capable of generating both speech and mel-spectrograms conditioned on trait inputs. Additionally, we present a new dataset, the University of Pennsylvania English Adolescent and Adult Speech (UPEEAS) corpus, which features annotated age-based and style-marked rhotacism for the social trait of interest. Experiments confirm that our proposed trait encoding mechanism is effective, as evidenced by our ability to synthesize conditioned speech and mel-specs. We further demonstrate that a VAM trained on this data outperforms a standard VAM in terms of generation quality.

We introduce a novel light dark matter framework featuring a dark sector characterized by $U(1)_D$ gauge symmetry and dark-charged fermions. The dark photon acquires mass via symmetry breaking driven by a complex scalar doublet, while dark fermions gain their masses through interactions with tetraquarks composed of four quarks in a color-singlet state. This specific quark composition ensures the requisite dark fermion charge assignments for compatibility with current experimental constraints. The model's symmetries, including $U(1)_{B-L}$ and a discrete $A_4$ group, enable the radiative generation of neutrino masses, yielding predictions that align with observed oscillation data. Additionally, the framework predicts several new particles and associated phenomena at the LHC, offering distinct avenues for future verification.

This work investigates the collective dynamics of triaxial nuclei by applying the Bohr Hamiltonian, which is modified through a minimal length framework to ensure compliance with Heisenberg's uncertainty relations. Within this modified structure, the potential energy term adopts a Pöschl-Teller form to account for three distinct collective modes: $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $\delta$. The resulting modified equations for $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are solved using a perturbative approach to handle the $\delta$ component, which remains small. Energy eigenvalues and corresponding wave functions are derived for the triaxial nucleus, and E2 transition probabilities are calculated to compare the findings with experimental data for the well-studied nucleus $^{166}$Er.

This paper introduces new constructions of polyphase Golay complementary arrays (pGCAs) for dimensions $d \ge 2$. Specifically, we present a pGCA design for complex exponential arrays of size $M^d \times d$ using four phases, real-valued pGCAs of length $M^d \times d$ with two phases, and additional complex pGCAs of length $M^d \times d$ with four phases. Additionally, we establish sufficient conditions for constructing complex-valued pGCAs of length $M^d \times d$ with four phases.

Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is crucial for monitoring environmental shifts, such as urban development and deforestation. This study introduces an unsupervised deep learning framework for identifying pixel-level changes in high-dimensional hyperspectral images (HSI) by leveraging feature fusion within a 3D convolutional neuromodulator architecture. The method extracts salient features from two coregistered HSI pairs using deep convolutional layers, fuses these features to pinpoint alterations, and employs a neuromodulator to enhance the representation of binary change maps. Evaluated on three HSI datasets, the unsupervised approach demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional change detection techniques.

This study examines molecular fluids and Lennard-Jones (LJ) potentials to investigate the link between residual entropy and viscosity. Entropy calculations utilized the Gibbs-Boltzmann framework, while viscosity was estimated via the Green-Kubo relation. Simulations employed the NVT ensemble with the Nosé-Hoover thermostat. Results indicate that for both LJ and molecular models, residual entropy correlates linearly with viscosity. Furthermore, both LJ and molecular fluids display a comparable relationship between residual entropy and reduced viscosity. These findings suggest that molecular fluid complexity does not disrupt the fundamental connection between residual entropy and viscosity.

Keyphrase Spotting (KPS) is a task focused on automatically identifying relevant keyphrases within captions for specific query passages. While Neural Networks (NNs) have achieved top-tier results on keyphrase detection for standard desktop systems, they remain unsuitable for IoT devices due to their high computational demands. This paper introduces a lightweight neural network architecture designed to deliver competitive accuracy on captioned queries while maintaining efficiency. Our approach utilizes a BERT-based encoder to process captions and an LSTM-based decoder to generate keyphrases. Experimental results demonstrate that this BERT-LSTM configuration achieves a recall of 0.408, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art accuracy of 0.388. Additionally, the proposed architecture offers a favorable balance between computational efficiency and performance, making it well-adapted for deployment on resource-constrained IoT hardware.

This field is expressed through holonomies, which are unitary matrices assigned to gauge links. We demonstrate that the partition function for this system, denoted as $Z_{\rm dimer}$, can be derived from a fermionic model, $Z_{\rm fermion}$, by applying a local gauge transformation. In this mapping, the fermionic action $S_{\rm fermion}$ is related to the dimer energy via $Z_{\rm fermion} = Z_{\rm dimer} \langle \exp(i S_{\rm fermion}) \rangle$. The study reveals that the expectation value of the fermionic term $\langle \exp(i S_{\rm fermion}) \rangle$ vanishes whenever the topological charge of the gauge field is non-zero. Consequently, the dimer partition function becomes zero in regimes where such a background field exists. The hypervisor facilitates running multiple virtual machines (VMs) concurrently, each hosting a distinct guest operating system. This approach offers significant advantages in embedded systems, particularly by enhancing system isolation and maintainability. Nevertheless, legacy hypervisors often lack the strict real-time performance guarantees essential for modern applications. To address this, the paper introduces T-Visor, a Type-1 hypervisor built upon Intel's Virtualization Technology (VT). This solution supports scheduling mixed-criticality real-time tasks across both physical machines and VMs. By leveraging the x86 architecture's hardware scheduling mechanisms, T-Visor delivers robust performance and stability. Comprehensive evaluations confirm that the system effectively achieves its design goals of strong isolation and real-time capability.

Solving the Panoptic Stitching problem involves reconstructing a complete, seamless panorama from a set of overlapping images, where the input consists of a graph with each node representing a photograph. We introduce a new algorithm that leverages a gravity-based pre-alignment strategy to rapidly identify the minimum Steiner solution within this panoramic framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces significantly faster outcomes compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining equivalent reconstruction accuracy.

This study investigates the synchronization dynamics of a composite chimera within a minimal framework consisting of two identical, variably coupled groups of identical phase oscillators. The resulting system exhibits a unique chimera state characterized by two coexisting clusters: one displays uniform phase synchronization, while the other features an anti-phase relationship with its own internally coherent group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the emergence of chimera behavior is sustained even when uniform variabilities are introduced into the coupling between the two populations.

This study addresses the challenge of learning control policies for linear time-invariant systems interacting with stochastic environments. We introduce a novel learning-based method that integrates probabilistic system modeling with a policy optimization framework. This approach ensures robust performance in the face of environmental uncertainties. The core methodology involves utilizing a probabilistic model-based policy gradient technique to directly optimize for a learning-based policy constrained by a probabilistic model of the system dynamics. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for the gradient of policy with respect to the underlying system model. We demonstrate that our method offers a distinct advantage: it achieves sample complexity that is polynomial relative to the dimension of the policy function approximator and independent of the policy's policy space's complexity, a significant improvement over prior work. We also provide a formal convergence analysis for the proposed algorithm. Empirical evaluations across control tasks featuring stochastic environments and nonlinear dynamics substantiate the method's efficacy.

Random tensor networks (RTNs) serve as a compelling framework for investigating quantum entanglement within holographic systems. This study focuses on RTNs that support a specific class of operators, termed *reflected information*, which quantifies how much data about one such an operator can be accessed through a complementary region's multiple copies. We establish an efficient calculation method for reflected information in RTNs by leveraging the geometry of generalized Petz maps. Additionally, we derive general theoretical bounds for an extensive set of scenarios and demonstrate how reflected information behaves in various RTN configurations.

Although living cells are inherently noisy, they utilize random fluctuations to drive diverse processes essential for life, from facilitating protein folding to enabling cellular movement and driving gene expression switches. This work investigates how genetic material can be transmitted alongside robust, stable spatiotemporal patterns during the development of multicellular organisms. We introduce a theoretical framework where hereditary information is encoded within a time-delayed feedback loop that regulates gene expression in a growing one-dimensional cell chain. By analyzing this model under conditions of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic development, we demonstrate that a specific combination of feedback delays and cellular division rates allows reliable inheritance of stable patterns across generations. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics occurring at a newly formed cell boundary and the resulting impact on pattern stability. These findings offer a new perspective on how living cells harness noise to generate stable dynamical behaviors that persist through lineage division.

The generalized Hénon three-dimensional model is a nonlinear dynamical system defined by the equations $x_{n+1} = F(x_n, y_n, z_n)$, $y_{n+1} = \alpha x_n - \beta z_n - \gamma F(x_n, y_n, z_n)$, and $z_{n+1} = \beta x_n - \gamma y_n$. This system extends the well-known two-dimensional quadratic map, $x_{n+1} = \alpha x_n - \beta y_n^2$ and $y_{n+1} = \epsilon + \beta x_n^2 - \mu n$, by incorporating an additional dimension and modifying the functional form. In this study, we analyze the dynamics of the new three-dimensional model, specifically focusing on the geometric structures of its attractors. We employ both numerical simulations and analytical methods to characterize these dynamics. The results indicate that the system undergoes a period-doubling bifurcation as control parameters are varied, leading to the emergence of complex fractal structures. We also explore the relationship between the basin of attraction and the fractal dimension of the attractor.

We establish a refined, fine-scale version of the Fine-Ng\^o theorem by establishing the exact constant in the limiting density function for squares of hook lengths summed over partitions divisible by two. Additionally, we analyze the third-moment distribution for partitions divisible by three. We demonstrate a refined, fine-scale version of the Fine-Ng\^o theorem by establishing the exact constant in the limiting density function for hook lengths squared across partitions that are multiples of two. Our work further investigates the distribution of hook lengths cubed for partitions divisible by three, providing a complete analysis of the third-moment distribution in this context.

We introduce a way to measure tunneling time by monitoring spin fluctuations through a Larmor clock, a method whose accuracy is ensured by a theoretically sound definition of tunneling time. The study reveals that when a particle encounters a barrier with a spin-flip component, it exhibits spin precession and fluctuations that allow us to define the tunneling duration specifically as the average time spent in the region where spin orientation changes. The Heisenberg-Wigner time delay is identified as a specific case of this approach, applicable only when the barrier induces a pure phase shift. The work also demonstrates that the mean dwell time is insufficient to fully characterize the process, as it fails to account for the distinct behaviors of particles with different spin states.

We derive the leading-twist distribution functions for these particles, which are subsequently utilized to calculate the structure functions of the $J/\psi$ during deep virtual and deep virtual photoproduction processes.

The study examines a Bose-Einstein condensate characterized by nonlinear interactions, with its dynamics modeled using Gross-Pitaevskii and Schrödinger equations. While the initial conditions are defined by quantum Gaussian wave packets, the evolution of these operators within the quantum framework is analyzed. Notably, new nonlinear quantum operators emerge that map linear creation and annihilation operators into their nonlinear counterparts.

The asymptotic symmetries of Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) spacetime have been identified as a potential framework for characterizing the infrared sector of asymptotically flat theories. This perspective offers two primary avenues for characterizing such regions: first, by examining how radiation influences bms-invariant observables, and second, by utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence to map the BMS geometry onto a dual conformal field theory. This dual description facilitates a clearer understanding of soft theorems and their associated phases. Specifically, we demonstrate that the leading soft graviton theorem corresponds to the insertion of soft charges in correlation functions, while the subleading soft graviton theorem maps to the insertion of the Beltrami operator, which deforms the complex structure of the BMS sphere. Furthermore, the phase factors inherent in these operators are shown to arise from worldline effects.

Continual learning (CL) focuses on training models incrementally on a sequence of tasks while maintaining the ability to recall previous knowledge. This field is particularly vital for real-world applications where data arrives in real-time and task labels are often unavailable. This study examines CL from an online learning perspective, where the model updates continuously as new data streams in, rather than using batch retraining. Unlike online learning, however, CL requires the system to adapt to distinct new tasks while preventing catastrophic forgetting of old ones. This paper introduces an online ensemble framework designed to address these challenges. The approach utilizes a specialized neural architecture that integrates multiple online learners within a hierarchical structure. Each learner trains sequentially on incoming data, and a dedicated recurrent module aggregates their outputs to form the final prediction. Empirical results demonstrate that this online ensemble method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and training efficiency.

We return to the study of differential forms generalized to higher measures and their associated Riccicurvatures. By examining the case of four-measures on a classical Riemannian manifold, we reconstruct the metric, demonstrate that Ricci-flatness corresponds to the Ricci-tensor four-measures being zero, and discuss implications for Einstein manifolds. Additionally, we extend this framework to include differential forms of degree greater than one.

This study examines the properties of two distinct types of polynomials over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$: permutation polynomials and total permutation polynomials. The first category maps every element of the field to a unique value within the field, whereas the second maps elements such that both the resulting value and its corresponding image in the multiplicative group $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}^*$ are also unique. By analyzing the specific structure of $f(x,y,z) = x^a y^b z^c + x y^{a'} y^{b'} y^{c'} + \dots$, we focus on monomials combined with trinomial forms like $x^a y^b z^c + x y^{a'} y^{b'} y^{c'} + \dots$, where $a,b,c,a',b',c'$ are integers. We derive the precise conditions required for these functions to exhibit the permutation property and establish their behavior under various parameter configurations. Additionally, we explore connections between these polynomials and planar functions, highlighting shared structural traits.

Intestinal parasites are a prevalent global health issue, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Their presence can be detected through microscopic examination of stool samples, a technique known as coproscopy. In this coproscopic process, a laboratory technician analyzes the sample to identify and classify parasite eggs, which are referred to as "cysts." The primary challenge in cyst categorization is the scarcity of available training data. To address this, we propose a Deep Belief Network (DBN) approach for cyst categorization. Our findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

This research examines an asymptotic non-zero-sum game involving two firms, where each company manages risk exposure through investment and reinsurance strategies. The risk dynamics for both firms are modeled using coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations (HJIEs) within a regime-switching jump-diffusion environment. To address these HJIES, we introduce a singularly perturbed stochastic differential equation (SDE) that drives the underlying system. By leveraging the weak convergence of controlled diffusion processes alongside stochastic maximum principles, we establish the existence of a viscosity solution for the associated asymptotic HJIE. Furthermore, we develop a finite-difference approximation scheme to numerically compute these viscosity solutions. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through a concrete numerical example.

This study introduces a novel dual-arm cooperative control method designed for smooth and stable payload lifting. First, a probabilistic dual-arm simplex algorithm (PIDA) is developed to regulate the joint movements of the two robotic arms. Unlike traditional approaches, PIDA utilizes a two-dimensional search space to determine the two degrees of freedom for payload positioning, which streamlines the optimization process. Second, a dedicated payload force estimator is implemented to calculate the force exerted on the object. This estimator employs a new Genetic Filter that integrates a specific fitness function with a dedicated mutation strategy to ensure rapid and precise convergence. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, demonstrating significant improvements in achieving stable and smooth dual-arm cooperation.

This study examines low-energy pion-nucleon interactions, emphasizing their role as a critical probe into the fundamental properties of the nuclear force. By utilizing dispersion relations, researchers can derive the complex, energy-dependent pion-nucleon scattering amplitude from experimentally accessible quantities such as total cross sections and optical potentials. A key focus is placed on the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance, which dominates the scattering amplitude in the isospin $I=3/2$ channel. Consequently, a comprehensive analysis of the $\Delta$ resonance is conducted to determine its mass, width, and the characteristics of the non-resonant background. Furthermore, the paper investigates how the $\Delta$ resonance and its associated background influence low-energy parameters, including the scattering lengths and effective ranges for both $S$-wave channels.

CMS is an experiment designed to search for new physics beyond the Standard Model and to measure fundamental properties of the Higgs boson and the Standard Model particles. The detector's innermost component is the Pixel Detector, which provides high-resolution tracking of charged particles produced in proton-proton collisions. Following a major upgrade to prepare for LHC Run 3 and higher luminosity operations, CMS is currently installing the reconfigured system. This article details the software used to reconstruct the newly designed Pixel Pilot Blades, which serve as temporary tracking during the installation phase.

Short-range correlations (SRCs) within nuclei represent a complex multi-body phenomenon that necessitates a sophisticated theoretical framework for description. This study examines various phase-space representations to capture SRC effects, including the Wigner function, the Husimi function, and the Wigner Husimi distribution, alongside the associated numerical challenges. We illustrate the application of these methods to the two-body density of the deuteron and the three-body density of the triton, demonstrating how the resulting features can be utilized to construct a phase-space framework for modeling deuteron-like SRC correlations in multi-nucleon systems.

This study addresses complex-valued equality issues within deep learning, a domain that has received minimal attention compared to its real-valued counterpart. We introduce a novel architecture capable of producing complex outputs and demonstrate that conventional equality checks fail in this context due to inherent data characteristics. Furthermore, we examine complex-valued equality from multiple perspectives, including the impact of floating-point representation errors. To resolve this, we propose a specialized Complex-Valued Equality Layer designed to accurately validate complex numbers in deep neural networks.

This work examines the latest advancements in the saturation of gluon densities within the context of the nuclear gluon structure function, $g^A(x,Q^2)$. It explores the implications of geometrical scaling observed in neutral-current deep inelastic scattering off nuclei and its connection to the saturation of gluon densities. Additionally, the study analyzes the behavior of the saturation momentum, $Q_{sat}^A$, as a function of the Bjorken variable $x$ and the nuclear mass number $A$, alongside a comparison of $Q_{sat}^A$ predictions from various models against experimental data. The article also reviews the status of saturation in heavy ion collisions, specifically focusing on the production of soft hadrons and the emergence of the ridge phenomenon.

We investigate the origins of amplitude dispersion in low-metallicity stars by analyzing 1,000 pulsating models of Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars, which span a range of masses (0.45–0.80 M$_{\odot}$), luminosities (1000–6000 L$_{\odot}$), and effective temperatures (2500–3200 K). Our findings indicate that this amplitude scatter is primarily driven by the ratio of pulsation period to the thermal timescale, rather than by the specific values of mass, temperature, or metallicity. Furthermore, the data reveal that the variability amplitude increases with temperature for stars that share the same pulsation period.

This study introduces a novel toolbox designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning models, which is critical for ensuring the reliability of learning algorithms. We apply this toolbox to measure how financial literacy scores influence machine learning predictions regarding individuals' wealth levels. Our analysis reveals that while financial literacy scores significantly impact the prediction of wealth levels, these predictions remain robust against variations in specific scoring mechanisms used for financial literacy.

This study introduces a novel framework termed "SQUID" for quantum neural networks, which leverages the specific properties of SQUIDs—the foundational components of superconducting quantum processors. The architecture integrates the creation and manipulation of quantum states, the generation of quantum gates, and the execution of quantum variational algorithms. Specifically, the system employs Josephson junctions to produce nonlinear activation functions, while the dynamics of the circuit's inductive and capacitive elements serve as the polynomial activation functions and neurons, respectively. Distinctively, within this model, the creation of gates and the preparation of initial quantum states are performed without loss of quantumness. Consequently, SQUID offers a streamlined and efficient methodology for building quantum neural networks. The authors validate this approach by implementing a basic yet illustrative example: a binary classifier designed to distinguish between ground and flux states of a Josephson junction.

Warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds are explored within the framework of almost contact manifolds. This study specifically examines the conditions required to realize such structures via isometric products in warped forms, with a focus on the geometry of the warped product pointwise semiinclination.

The PALEOCCENE framework represents a proposed low-energy threshold approach utilizing the color centers found in crystalline silicon. It is designed to remain resilient against various background sources, specifically including the 2.5 keV gamma emissions from $^{55}$Fe and $^{55}$Co, as well as thermal noise. This study details the PALEOCCENE strategy and presents initial experimental validation from a 200 mm silicon wafer detector, which achieved an effective threshold of approximately 0.7 eV. This work also examines the impact of multiple operational parameters on the device's noise floor.

Colloidal molecules consist of multiple particles bound by interparticle forces, and their internal dynamics are significantly altered when immersed in active suspensions. This study investigates the behavior of a two-particle colloidal molecule within a background of active Brownian particles, focusing on how activity gradients influence it. Specifically, we examine the role of the relative orientation between the dipole moment and the center-of-mass activity of the molecule. Our findings reveal that these parameters dictate whether the suspending particles enhance or suppress the molecule's rotational diffusion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the molecule's internal structure can be actively controlled by manipulating the activity it experiences.

The magnetic field's influence on the internal structure of magnetorotons in the lowest Landau level of two-dimensional fractional quantum Hall systems is examined. This investigation reveals that the system's magnetic environment can induce multiple magnetoroton minima. By applying a rigorous theoretical framework, we establish two spectral sum rules governing the magnetorotron, which elucidate the mechanism behind the emergence of these additional minima.

This study examines the geometric characteristics of identifying epidemic outbreak clusters within networks. Specifically, it investigates how to effectively partition a network into communities, where each community corresponds to a distinct outbreak. The analysis demonstrates that this clustering problem can be modeled as a multi-class classification task. Furthermore, it proposes a generalized classification framework applicable to any network clustering method. The work also establishes that the proposed classifier is both necessary and sufficient for identifying the community structure generated by any minimization of modularity function. Additionally, it provides a criterion for determining when a given partition constitutes a modularity maximum.

This study examines the impact of X-source removal techniques on CMB maps derived from Planck data, utilizing a maximum likelihood approach. We analyze three methods: a Bayesian one-pixel-at-a-time strategy, a Bayesian multi-pixel strategy, and a frequentist method. The findings indicate that the Bayesian X-source removal approach demonstrates superior performance in minimizing residuals near bright point sources, specifically around Cas A. Furthermore, we assess the efficacy of these removal strategies in the context of B-mode polarization analysis.

"Reference resolution plays a crucial role in natural language processing and communication. However, creating artificial references to objects is labor-intensive and challenging in reinforcement learning (RL) environments. We introduce a procedure to characterize completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps utilizing a shadow technique. This method estimates the CPTP map by measuring specific observables on an extended system that incorporates an ancilla. The selected observables are those capable of estimating the weights associated with a chosen basis of shadow states. We demonstrate that, for a fixed number of measured shadows, our approach minimizes the estimation error for any specific channel feature. Furthermore, we establish that determining a CPTP map from experimental data necessitates a minimum quantity of repeated experiments that aligns with the theoretical lower bound.

This study focuses on the integral mean $\int_0^1 \check{\lambda}_0(\Omega_t) dt$ associated with the Cheeger factor of a planar convex domain $\Omega$. The authors establish a sharp upper limit for this integral mean, comparable to the sharp lower limit previously derived by Giusti and Maggi. The proof relies on establishing novel sharp bounds for the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian under Dirichlet boundary constraints within shrinking domains $\Omega_t = t\Omega$.

This study addresses the problem of optimizing path selection for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to minimize total travel distance while maintaining specific operational constraints. Unlike previous research that typically assumes fixed mission durations, our model focuses on time-constrained applications where the number of available slots is predetermined. We formalize this challenge as the Time Constrained UAV Path Optimization (TC-UPO) problem and establish its computational hardness by demonstrating that it is NP-hard. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm named UAV-LS for addressing TC-UPO. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing approaches by reducing total flight distance by 10% and decreasing runtime by 100% compared to the baseline.

We examine bilayer graphene within a renormalization group framework to investigate the effects of long-range Coulomb interactions. Our results indicate that the system remains stable against the formation of bilayer-specific instabilities, such as nematic phases. Instead, anisotropic scattering channels exhibit marginal relevance, meaning their impact is negligible compared to short-range models where nematic ordering emerges. This finding contrasts sharply with single-layer graphene, where the RG approach predicts strong tendencies toward nematicity.

The study utilizes scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to examine the conformational changes of the endofullerene Sc2TbN@C80 on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate as a function of temperature. The results reveal that heating causes a progressive shift in the preferred orientation of the molecule, ultimately resulting in a single-orientation state at elevated temperatures. Additionally, the research investigates the impact of temperature on the electronic structure of Sc2TbN@C80@h-BN/Ni(111) using ARPES. The findings indicate that temperature variations do not significantly alter the characteristic Jahn-Teller splitting of the LUMO band. These observations are further supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which validate the experimental data.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, connecting an increasing number of smart devices to the internet. Driven by the need for low-cost and energy-efficient solutions, these devices are increasingly adopted for security applications. However, traditional encryption algorithms are often too resource-intensive for the limited computational power and memory available in IoT architectures. This paper introduces a new compact encryption scheme designed specifically for Low Power IoT Devices (LP IoT). The proposed method utilizes a bijective function to generate a bijective matrix, which is then combined with a non-bijective vector to form a singular matrix for use in stream cipher encryption. The resulting singular matrix is integrated with a block cipher that relies on a bijective matrix and a non-bijective vector for a key schedule. The proposed algorithm demonstrates low computational complexity and minimal hardware footprint, making it well-suited for LP IoT devices.

This study introduces a sequential Bayesian experimental design that optimizes the measurement strategy for adaptive Ramsey sequences of free-induction decay, specifically for estimating an unknown phase. The proposed framework determines the most effective coherence time for each step, contingent upon the current uncertainty in the unknown phase. We demonstrate that this approach yields a higher average estimation accuracy than a non-adaptive method that employs a fixed total coherence time. Additionally, the experimentally accessible nature of the design parameters makes this protocol suitable for practical implementation in quantum technologies.

We introduce a novel network centrality metric termed Gromov Centrality (GOC), which leverages the triangle inequality excess to quantify a node's local geometric features based on shortest path distances. The GOC is mathematically derived from these geodesic paths and is computationally efficient, with a time complexity of $O(N^2)$ for a network of size $N$. The metric effectively captures multi-scale structural attributes, including local properties like degree and clustering coefficient, as well as global aspects such as betweenness and eigenvector centrality. Additionally, GOC serves as a bridge between local and global network topology through the Gromov distance. We demonstrate that GOC provides high predictive accuracy for node-level phenomena, including disease progression and the likelihood of information adoption, and is applicable to diverse domains ranging from epidemiology to finance.

This work introduces a new model of gravitation based on full tensor formalism featuring azimuthal symmetry. We employ a novel coordinate system defined by oblate spheroidal coordinates, utilizing full tensor formalism to ensure complete generality. Within this framework, the metric tensor is expressed as a function of three independent field variables that possess distinct physical meanings. A new field equation is proposed, derived from a corresponding field action, which reduces to the Einstein-Maxwell equations in the specific limit of vanishing variables. The model's validity is further demonstrated by deriving the field equations for both a point particle and a uniformly rotating sphere, with results aligning perfectly with existing physical theories.

We define the "bundle of matrix operators" as a collection consisting of a base space, a vector bundle, and a family of constant-sized matrix-valued operators that act linearly on the fibers of this vector bundle, subject to specific smoothness requirements. This study focuses on "strict equivalence," a relation between bundles formed by these matrices if they are isomorphic in a way that preserves the operator values pointwise. The work establishes the functorial nature of a functor that associates a bundle of these matrix operators with its underlying vector bundle. Additionally, a "local model" is introduced as a vector bundle equipped with a bundle of matrix operators that is smooth only up to the final stratum. It is demonstrated that any bundle of matrix operators can be constructed from a local model through a Whitney sum operation. The authors also define "elementary bundles" as those with rank one and trivial monodromy, proving that every bundle with vanishing monodromy is isomorphic to a direct sum of these elementary types. Finally, a formula is derived to calculate the dimension of the isomorphism class for strict equivalences, specifically for the local model, based on its monodromy data.
We introduce a new class of topological T-dual pairs consisting of topological torus bundles over topological, not necessarily trivial, torus bundles.

This study establishes that for strongly monotonic discrete-time dynamical systems with smooth mappings exhibiting a fixed point, the 2-cyclic behavior is prevalent. We also demonstrate that for convex strongly monotonic maps without periodic points, trajectories converge to the fixed point for every initial condition. These results represent extensions of the work by A. J. Negrini and A. Sontag, who addressed the continuous-time counterpart.

Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VVIE) are widely used for approximating ground states, but their efficiency is often hindered by a high count of variational parameters (VPs) and measurement cycles. This paper introduces an adaptive VP reduction strategy that leverages qubit-excitation properties to optimize circuit depth. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the number of required VPs is dictated by the qubit-excitation structure. We validate this approach using the molecular hydrogen (H2) system, showing that our method achieves comparable accuracy to standard VIEs while using 50% fewer variational parameters and completing execution 2.5 times faster.

Deep generative models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), are typically employed to learn latent representations for a given dataset. However, these models face challenges related to their expressive power and training efficiency. This work introduces the deep generative encoder (DG Encoder), a method that utilizes the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates derived from VAEs to represent data distributions. By applying this approach to VAEs, the DG Encoder enhances their representational capacity and achieves more efficient optimization. Experiments on various classification and regression datasets demonstrate that the DG Encoder surpasses standard autoencoder architectures in terms of both representation expressiveness and task accuracy.

We report the first ALMA Atacama Compact Array (ACA) observations of comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a distance of 1.1 AU, utilizing the 7 GHz Band 3D mode to survey the compact radio emission. The data reveal a source with a full width at half maximum of 1.1 arcseconds, which is consistent with a point source after correcting for the primary beam. We detected no significant flux variation relative to the nucleus as the beam swept across the coma, nor did we observe extended emission. These results indicate that the coma is not resolved by the primary beam, implying a physical size of less than 0.0004 pc (approximately 120 AU). This upper limit on the coma size is comparable to previous findings for the active comet C/2014 Q2 (Jewitt). Our non-detection of extended emission suggests that the outgassing of CS₂ is confined to a dispersed source rather than a singular point.

This study investigates a complex-based Holographic Dark Energy (HDE) framework incorporating a Tsallis non-extensive entropy, utilizing an essence model to explore the cosmological evolution of the universe. The proposed essence model, which utilizes complex field dynamics, is designed to replicate the transition from an early accelerated expansion to a subsequent late-time acceleration. This study introduces a branch-and-bound framework enhanced with NSGA-II to tackle multi-objective mixed-integer nonlinear optimization (MO-MINLO) challenges. The approach leverages the robust NSGA-II genetic algorithm for generating candidate solutions on both the objective and decision spaces. To manage constraints, the method employs the constraint ranking strategy, which orders individuals based on constraint violations. Population diversity is maintained through tournament selection, while the non-dominated sorting approach ranks solutions, and the fast non-dominated sort operator constructs the final front. The user preference for the solution set is addressed via the crowding distance metric. Within the main branch-and-bound loop, the estimated lower bound is calculated by relaxing the integer variables to continuous ones and solving the resulting problem using NSGA-II. The method's efficacy is validated against two case studies: a multi-objective production planning problem and a multi-objective facility location problem.

This paper demonstrates within the framework of Synthetic Differential Geometry (SDG) that internal connected Lie groupoids in SDG models are integral complete and possess an internal linkage. Specifically, we establish an internal variant of the theorem by Connes and Gambier, which asserts that internal connected Lie groups are linkage internal and integrally complete. These findings have significant implications for SDG approaches to differential geometry, topology, and the theory of differential equations.

The rapid expansion of biomedical datasets has created a critical need for efficient data sharing to support collaborative research. However, numerous obstacles impede this process, including data silos, restricted access, and privacy concerns. To address these challenges, we introduce a gateway-based architecture designed to enable secure and seamless sharing of biomedical data. This solution integrates diverse data sources from various repositories and institutions, granting users secure entry points to access and analyze the information. We have implemented and tested this architecture through a dedicated gateway within a cyberinfrastructure environment.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) aims to determine the emotional polarity of specific parts within an opinion holder relative to those aspects. While recent advances have largely focused on enhancing semantic understanding through pre-training, this study introduces a new approach centered on modeling implicit emotions in ABSA tasks. We propose a new model, SUPERCOP-IE, which integrates the implicit emotion pre-training objective into the SUPERCOP framework. Specifically, SUPERCOP-IE employs a masked emotion prediction task to identify implicit emotions within aspect-holder opinion pairs. Additionally, we introduce the OP-IE dataset, derived from the OPinion-IEnc (OP-IE) domain, to facilitate this pre-training phase. Experimental results demonstrate that SUPERCOP-IE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both implicit and explicit sentiment analysis benchmarks.

This study investigates robust secure resource allocation for reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided networks affected by hardware impairments. The objective is to maximize the minimum secrecy capacity across users, subject to the practical constraints of unitary matrix properties, active and passive power limits, and hw impairment characteristics. To address these challenges, a joint active and passive robust beamforming strategy is developed. First, the problem is reformulated as an equivalent convex optimization task. Subsequently, an iterative algorithm is proposed to determine the optimal robust active and passive beamforming vectors. Finally, numerical simulations demonstrate that the suggested method outperforms conventional schemes lacking RIS assistance or considering hardware impairments.

This study introduces a novel reinforcement learning method termed Contrastive Executive Function (CEF), which draws inspiration from human cognitive processes. Specifically, CEF mimics how individuals utilize an "executive function" to gather, evaluate, and prioritize diverse goals by dynamically adjusting learning through the sampling and re-labeling of self-generated experiences. At its core lies a contrastive value strategy designed to assess the relationship between experience pairs, enabling the selective focus on high-value, unique, and diverse data points. Additionally, the approach employs an hindsight contrastive natural language processing model to generate detailed summaries for each experience, facilitating more precise value estimations and the adaptive refinement of labeling accuracy. Empirical evaluations across three distinct tasks demonstrate that CEF achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-theart reinforcement learning algorithms.

Solar wind energy flux, which drives the heating of the solar corona, remains a subject of significant debate. This flux is typically measured in the inner heliosphere using the total heating rate of the solar wind plasma. We report the first measurements of solar wind energy flux derived from Parker Solar Probe data, covering heliocentric distances between 15 and 33.5 $R_{\odot}$. Our analysis reveals that the energy budget is dominated by the thermal energy of protons, while the kinetic energy of the bulk flow and magnetic energy are negligible. Furthermore, we observe that the radial gradient of the proton thermal energy dominates the calculation of the energy flux. This finding suggests that the solar corona is heated primarily by mechanisms operating at the scale of the proton mean free path.

We offer a noncommutative generalization of topological principal bundles in the context of free countable group actions on C*-algebras. Specifically, we define a topological space $X$, a countable group $\Gamma$, and a continuous action $\gamma: \Gamma \to \mathcal{P}(X)$, constructing the associated bundle as the pullback of the crossed product C*-algebra $\gamma \ltimes C(X)$ over the group C*-algebra $C(\Gamma)$, assuming freeness. We establish that when this action is free, the resulting bundle is a locally trivial fiber bundle with structure group $\Gamma$. Furthermore, we examine properties such as local triviality, smoothness, and connections within this noncommutative framework.

This study explores fast and slow light propagation within a $q$-deformed optomechanical system featuring a resonator-coupled linear oscillator. By analyzing the linear response of the system, we investigate fast and slow light phenomena based on the group velocity of probe light. Our findings indicate that the non-conventional deformation in the optomechanical setup can enhance the clarity of these phenomena. Additionally, we demonstrate that the system offers superior control over fast and slow light effects compared to standard optomechanical models.

This research investigates the Two-Rotor Model under R-parity breaking conditions, specifically examining the "scissors mode" within a perturbative approach. We demonstrate that introducing a scissors-like oscillation as a third degree of freedom results in the original scissors mode splitting into two distinct modes of the same R-parity. Notably, the mode possessing the lower energy lacks a well-defined wave function in the strict perturbative limit. Furthermore, we establish that the anomalous R-matrix pole responsible for this mode aligns with the predictions of the collective model.

This study introduces a cell-based mean neural network approach for resolving hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. The method involves partitioning the domain into cells and utilizing neural networks to approximate the cell-averaged values across the solution space. A key advantage of this technique is its ability to achieve high accuracy with a significantly reduced number of parameters compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, by employing a specialized loss function, the approach ensures the stability of the neural network solution. The proposed methodology is validated through numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear equations, demonstrating its efficacy on instances such as the linear advection equation, Burger's equation, the heat equation, and the semi-linear heat equation.

The LHC is currently operating with a design collision energy of 5.3 TeV per beam, which is significantly lower than its previous peak of 13 TeV. This reduction is necessitated by the need to upgrade the accelerator's superconducting magnets to withstand higher currents for enhanced performance. To further enhance the ALICE experiment's capabilities in studying heavy-ion collisions, the collaboration plans to install a new solenoid magnet with 3.5 Tesla strength. This upgrade will expand the experiment's reach for high-multiplicity events and enable precise measurements of heavy quark production, even at lower energies. This article outlines the proposed enhancements to ALICE, detailing the magnet specifications, detector upgrades, and simulation results that demonstrate the anticipated improvements in physics performance.

We investigate the relationship between the Berry phase and the timelike Unruh effect within Rindler coordinates. By modeling a quantum particle moving along timelike geodesics in this coordinate system, we demonstrate that the geometric phase acquired by future and past light cones manifests as timelike rotations, mirroring the action of the timelike Unruh effect. Consequently, the acquisition of the Berry phase by such a particle serves as an operational signature of the timelike Unruh phenomenon.

Disaster response relies heavily on quickly identifying and processing critical information from social media. While numerous studies address this challenge, they predominantly focus on English, leaving a significant gap in handling other languages. This limitation is problematic given that global disasters often occur in non-English speaking regions. To address this, we introduce the Multilingual Incident Extraction (MEE) dataset, which is the first of its kind to categorize social posts into specific incident types based on geography and language. We evaluate various models, including BERT and BERTweet, using this dataset. Our analysis reveals that while English social media is highly effective for detecting incidents, it is less reliable in non-English contexts.

It is demonstrated that the Chern class associated with the direct image of a vector bundle remains positively curved whenever the original vector bundle possesses positive curvature. Furthermore, this result is generalized to scenarios involving the direct sum of multiple such bundles with individually positive curvature."

This study investigates the stellar breeze's impact on the hard X-ray emission and variability of Cyg X-1. We analyzed data from the XMM-Newton mission, obtained on 2011-05-11, using both XSPEC for spectral analysis and XTT for timing studies. The spectral modeling revealed that the stellar breeze's influence is negligible in the hard state. However, timing analysis of the 2-4 keV band uncovered a significant, periodic modulation at 2.6 days, matching the source's orbital period. This signal is absent in the 20-30 keV band, suggesting that the breeze does not drive the hard X-ray flux variations. Furthermore, cross-correlation between the 2-4 keV and 20-30 keV bands shows no evidence of orbital modulation. We conclude that the stellar breeze has no substantial effect on hard X-ray emission or timing behavior during Cyg X-1's hard state.

We propose a new model for parsing meaning that performs universal syntax parsing alongside semantic role parsing in a single, unified process. By leveraging shared syntactic patterns to model the meaning structure, our approach ensures that semantic parsing remains robust even when encountering previously unseen syntax. Our results indicate that our joint model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art systems dedicated solely to either universal syntax or semantic role parsing. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the shared syntax serves as a powerful inductive bias, significantly reducing the amount of data required for effective learning in semantics.

We examine magnetized, neutrino-cooled accretion disks that form following the merger of compact objects, such as black holes or neutron stars. These disks are hypothesized to drive jets via magnetocentrifugal processes, including Blandford-Payne and Blandford-Znajek mechanisms. Our study focuses on the jet generation phase involving the interaction between the disk's magnetic field and the neutrino-cooled outflow. We employ 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model a magnetized disk accreting onto a black hole, utilizing a neutrino transport scheme to account for the effects of neutrino cooling. Our results indicate that the outflow possesses a jet component, which is characterized by higher specific angular momentum and a lower degree of magnetization compared to the primary outflow. We analyze the characteristics of this secondary jet and its physical relationship with the outflow component.

We investigate the merger history of early-type galaxies (ETGs) by analyzing 1,000 objects with effective radii $R_e \leq 10$ kpc and stellar masses $10^{10.5} \leq \log(M_*/M_\odot) \leq 12.5$ using HSC-SSP138 data. By applying a novel segmentation method to identify tidal features, we measured their flux fractions and found that, for a fixed stellar mass, the mean tidal flux is higher in low-surface-brightness ETGs than in high-surface-brightness ones. These findings indicate that ETGs with $10^{10.5} \leq \log(M_*/M_\odot) \leq 11.5$ retain evidence of recent major mergers within the last 100 Myr. Additionally, we estimated the merger rate by comparing the observed flux fraction to theoretical light-curve models of tidal features. Our results suggest that low-mass ETGs undergo major mergers at a rate of $0.015$ per Gyr, while high-mass ETGs do so at $0.001$ per Gyr.

It focuses on the study of bipolar outflows as a repulsive gravitational phenomenon. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense millisecond-long radio signals of extragalactic origin. While their origins remain uncertain, leading theories suggest they arise from extreme events involving young neutron stars or black holes. This study reports the results of optical follow-up observations for 10 well-defined FRBs detected by the CHIME/HYDRA array, utilizing the 1.2-m telescope at the Apache Point Observatory. These observations were conducted using narrow-band filters to specifically target the Ca II H&K lines and the H-alpha line, aiming to detect potential optical counterparts. No optical emission was found in the immediate vicinity of the FRB signals for any of the FRBs studied. Additionally, searches for delayed optical flashes—specifically those occurring within 100 seconds of the radio burst—also yielded no results. These findings place stringent upper limits on the occurrence rates of both prompt and delayed optical counterparts for FRBs.

This research focuses on the reverse engineering of high-power laser systems, along with their design and enhancement. We introduce a unified framework designed to model the physical characteristics of these devices, facilitating their analysis and optimization. We also examine the inverse problem associated with system design, specifically how to derive a configuration that yields a desired output intensity profile. Additionally, we explore methods for system enhancement by integrating new components into existing architectures. Numerical examples are provided to validate these findings.

While recent research highlights the visual comprehension capabilities of visual language models, emerging evidence suggests that pre-trained text-only large language models can also be leveraged for visual tasks. This study demonstrates a straightforward approach to integrating visual inputs into such models by utilizing the visual encoding capabilities of established vision-language frameworks. Specifically, we extract visual features from CLIP and ResNet architectures to condition the text generation of GPT-3 on an observation of these images. This method enables GPT-3 to perform zero-shot image captioning and visual question answering effectively, without any fine-tuning. Notably, this approach achieves performance surpassing current state-of-the-art specialized models, all within the same computational cost as standard text applications. Furthermore, we observe that GPT-3 can generate multi-turn conversational responses regarding images, demonstrating an aptitude for sustained dialogue.
This paper introduces a modified RingCT scheme that reduces the verification time per transaction by a factor equivalent to the number of participating signature blinding proofs.

This study introduces a novel technique for beam diagnostics utilizing scans of the output brightness. The brightness of a transmitted beam is measured at the output of a scatterer as its position and orientation are systematically varied. The brightness is defined as the scalar product of the transmitted electric field and the complex conjugate of the incident electric field. The scan process is repeated across multiple points along the incident beam path. The brightness at each location is calculated by integrating the transmitted power through an aperture that is significantly smaller than the transmitted beam width but still large relative to the diffraction limit. The brightness scan is performed using a fixed aperture mask, which can take the form of either a single or a pair of slits. The resulting brightness data versus mask position is analyzed to determine the polarization state, power, and wavefront characteristics of the beam at each incident point. The analysis employs an extended version of the Stokes parameters to characterize polarization and a complex wavefront parameter vector to describe wavefront distortions. The incident beam's power is derived from the relationship between the measured brightness and the known aperture transmission efficiency. The proposed method is validated through numerical simulations and experimental verification using a laser beam.

This paper introduces a collaborative framework for constructing data-driven reduced-order models (ROMs) of large-scale systems, addressing the substantial data requirements that render traditional reduced-order modeling difficult. By enabling multiple data collectors to independently gather data from the same system at different locations or times, the proposed approach facilitates the creation of high-fidelity reduced-order models. We present a collaborative ROm framework that integrates data from multiple sources to build accurate representations of high-fidelity models. We also describe a specific method for combining these distributed datasets. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the error between the resulting model and the original system, demonstrating that this approach can generate models superior to those created using a single data source. Numerical examples are provided to validate the efficacy of the proposed framework.

The Feshbach-Schwinger mechanism predicts that the $\Upsilon(10753)$ resonance is a molecular state composed of $\Upsilon(5S)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(5S)\pi^0$. This study examines the decay process $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ within the framework of the hadronic loop mechanism. By employing the Bethe-Salpeter equation, we derive the wave function for the $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ hadronic loop. Consequently, we calculate the branching fractions for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ for $n=1,2,3,4,5,6$.
