We propose a simple yet effective method for unsupervised domain adaptation in dense object detection, achieving a 50.7% mAP on the DASTER dataset. This approach relies on a pre-trained teacher model to generate pseudo-labels for the target domain, which are then optimized via a novel two-stage adaptation framework. First, we train a domain-specific feature extractor using the target domain's images and these pseudo-labels. Second, we fine-tune an adapted adapter model on the same target domain data to better align the learned features. This two-phase strategy ensures high-quality supervision throughout adaptation and yields state-of-the-art performance. Our complete implementation is available at https://github.com/1337-1337/1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1337-1

Dimensionality reduction is frequently employed to map high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space for visualization and analysis. Standard techniques like t-SNE and Single View (MDS) are designed for Euclidean data, whereas SNE is adapted for Spherical data, utilizing the Hypersphere as its manifold. However, SNE has notable limitations: it is computationally intensive, it cannot handle data with missing values, and it struggles with noisy datasets. To address these issues, we introduce a Spherical version of Manifold Learning (VMF-SNE), which incorporates the Variational Message Passing (SNE) framework. Our method is designed to process spherical data, retain sparsity to manage missing values, and utilize variational inference for efficient parameter estimation. We further develop a specialized loss function for spherical data and implement an iterative update scheme to fit VMF-SNE. Experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both computational speed and accuracy.

The Monte Carlo simulation of the fermion polaron within a fermionic bath is performed using a diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach. We compute polaron properties, including the ground state energy, effective mass, and quasiparticle residue, for a fermionic bath with varying densities and interaction strengths. The results are compared against the large- and small-coupling expansions, as well as the self-consistent second-Born approximation. We observe that the second-Born method is insufficient for capturing the polaron's effective mass, particularly in regimes of weak coupling.

This paper introduces a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing strategy for simulating fermionic Hamiltonians, specifically targeting ground state energy and the density matrix. The proposed method involves decomposing the Hamiltonian into a sum of $K$-qubit terms and applying analog gates via quantum phase estimation to each individual term. For the digital component, we utilize the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) framework, employing a parameterized ansatz that maps fermionic creation and annihilation operators to sequences of digital quantum gates. To enhance computational efficiency, we incorporate the qubit-embedding technique, which maps the physical system into a larger quantum lattice by introducing auxiliary spin-1/2 degrees of freedom. This approach allows the resulting embedded system to be solved using the digital emulation scheme. The effectiveness of the hybrid method is validated through simulations of the Hubbard model on both one- and two-dimensional square lattices, demonstrating that the hybrid analog-digital scheme successfully recovers the exact ground state energy and the corresponding density matrix.

Graph polynomials serve as essential tools for characterizing various properties of these structures. This paper examines a sequence of polynomials $G_G(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ associated with a graph $G$ containing $k$ connected components. We establish that if this polynomial sequence exhibits the property of being log-concave for every monomial, it imposes significant constraints on the graph itself. Specifically, we demonstrate that only disjoint unions of trees and single-edge graphs satisfy this strictest form of polynomial positivity. Additionally, we explore connections between these findings and recent developments regarding graph invariants derived from the Hadamard product operation.

The Veech curve $\mathcal{C}_{\text{Veech}}$ within moduli space of flat surfaces $\mathcal{H}(1,1)$ is defined as the closure of Teichmüller curves originating from a square-tiled torus. This study examines the locus $\text{L}(\mathcal{C}_{\text{Veeech}})$ formed by the $\mathbb{P}^1$-extensions of points on this curve, situated within a Grassmannian. The primary findings demonstrate that $\text{L}(\mathcal{C}_{\text{Veeech}})$ possesses the structure of a semialgebraic set and that its projection back into moduli space $\mathcal{H}(1,1)$ also results in a semialgebraic set.

The COVID-19 pandemic and the resulting restrictions have compelled numerous companies to adopt permanent remote work models, including within the IT sector. Agile frameworks, particularly Scrum, are widely adopted in software development, yet there is limited understanding of how remote execution influences project outcomes. This study examines the impact of the "Working From Home" (WFH) practice on Scrum projects, specifically analyzing its correlation with both subjective and objective measures of success. Using a mixed-method approach, the research first explores Scrum practitioners' perspectives on WFH through a survey of 108 participants to identify significant factors. These insights were subsequently integrated into a structural equation model (SEM) to validate relationships among constructs. Finally, the study employed a comparative analysis across 100 diverse WFH and non-WFH Scrum projects to assess differences in success rates. The findings indicate that while the "Daily Stand-up" meeting is the primary driver of Scrum success, the impact of "WFH" itself is statistically insignificant.

The Gau-Wu value refers to the greatest magnitude of an eigenvalue of a Hermitian matrix. This study derives exact formulas for the Gau-Wu values of specific $4\times 4$ arrowhead matrices and establishes the necessary conditions for these values. Additionally, the paper calculates the maximum eigenvalue of a particular $4\times 4$ symmetric matrix with a Toeplitz-like structure.

This study presents the measurement of elliptic flow ($v_2$) for decay electrons originating from charm-hadrons within central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. The data, collected by the ALICE experiment at the LHC, covers a midrapidity range of $|y| < 0.8$ and transverse momentum up to $p_{\rm T} \approx$ 20 GeV/$c$. The observed $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of $v_2$ for charm-decay electrons is notably lower than that of beauty-hadron and light-flavor electrons. This measurement is compared against predictions from various theoretical frameworks, including a parton-hadron-dual scattering model and a perturbative QCD approach. The results align well with the parton-hatron-dual scattering model, which predicts a similar suppression of $v_2$ for charm and beauty decays relative to light flavors due to the limited phase space available for the heavier quarks.

A recent paper introduced the concept of chromatic persistence, which assigns a multi-persistence diagram to a function $f: V \to \mathbb{R}$ on a graph $G=(V,E)$ by utilizing the chromatic complex of its underlying alpha-structure. This article extends that research by examining how the chromatic persistence of alpha-structures varies with changes in the parameter $t$. We establish that this persistence is stable with respect to the function $f$ for any fixed $t$, and we provide a theoretical lower bound for the corresponding persistence distance. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of chromatic persistence as the parameter $t$ tends to infinity.

This work investigates the performance gap between optimal and binary (on-off) power control in arbitrary topologies of $K$-user interference networks. We demonstrate that, under the assumption of SDOF as the target metric, the Extremal Gain of Benefit (GBo) for binary power control relative to optimal control scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding establishes a definitive lower bound on the potential benefit of using binary power control. The proof relies on a novel framework for analyzing ExtBo in general settings, which involves a rigorous re-examination of the underlying topological geometry.

This paper introduces a new approach to auditing, which is a critical area for ensuring the integrity of financial reporting. We define auditing as the process of examining the reliability of financial statements. We focus on auditing as a cognitive endeavor that involves classifying audit findings into specific categories based on their similarity. To achieve this categorization, we employ a formal concept analysis framework combined with an adaptable operator. This study also integrates the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence to account for uncertainty during classification tasks. By utilizing evidence from the operator itself, we derive evidence for classification and subsequently determine the most appropriate categories for specific audit findings. We illustrate the effectiveness of this methodology through a case study involving the classification of audit findings.

This work presents a constructive solution to the Strauss process within a compact metric space, utilizing a steething approach inspired by the Gibbs measure on the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$. The steething procedure is defined in the finite case through the measure's relationship to the Poisson process. Furthermore, the method is applicable to a broader class of compact metric spaces by employing the concept of conformal density.

This study examines how the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) alters particle commutation relations, thereby influencing the structure of Galilean and Lorentz groups. We demonstrate that the GUP-induced correction to the position-momentum commutator results in modified Galilean transformations, which become inconsistent with the principle of relativity. Consequently, to preserve the relativistic framework, we propose new transformation sets that remain independent of the parameter $\theta$ and align with the GUP-adjusted commutation relations.

This study addresses the challenge of scheduling a queue of tasks, each with variable processing times, across a set of concurrent software services that share a pool of computing resources. The objective is to minimize the average time until a task completes, known as response time. We examine two operational modes: single-task execution, where a service handles only one active job at a time, and multi-task execution, allowing multiple jobs per service. For the single-task scenario, we establish an optimal scheduling strategy. Regarding multi-task scenarios, we prove that a specific scheduling policy combined with a particular assignment of tasks to services guarantees optimality. Additionally, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean response time when utilizing single-task assignments under our optimal policy. Finally, we compare the single- versus multi-task approaches across various conditions, identifying the specific parameters under which one approach outperforms the other.

This research investigates the performance of a monopod hopping robot operating on soft ground. The investigation begins with a theoretical derivation of the robot's yielding soil model, followed by the creation of a corresponding simulator. The study then analyzes the effect of ground stiffness on the monopod's residual velocity and total energy loss. Furthermore, the text outlines the implementation of an active control strategy to mitigate energy dissipation, demonstrating that this approach can reduce energy loss by up to 50% compared to yielding without support.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with applications ranging from industrial and medical fields to smart homes. A critical function within these domains is firmware updating, which is essential for ensuring security, reliability, and longevity. However, current update methods often fail to account for the unique characteristics of large-scale IoT deployments, specifically the communication protocols and infrastructure designed for such environments. This study investigates firmware distribution over a massive IoT mesh network, analyzing the impact of update strategies on performance metrics like network throughput, packet loss, and device latency. The research evaluates how concurrent updates affect performance across various conditions, including different network sizes, update adoption rates, and traffic patterns. Furthermore, the authors introduce a novel analytical model that accurately reflects the observed performance dynamics. These findings offer valuable guidance for engineers and researchers developing robust, dependable update mechanisms for the evolving IoT landscape.

This work examines the evolution of the single-particle eigenstate Fock-space propagator as the interaction strength $U$ increases toward the many-body localization (MBL) transition in the one-dimensional Hubbard model. Utilizing a tensor network algorithm, we compute the Fock-space propagator alongside the eigenstate entanglement entropy to determine the MBL critical value $U_c$ for both half-filling ($n=2$) and ($n=1.5$) cases. Our findings reveal that the Fock-space propagator scales as a power of the distance in Fock space, with an extracted multifractal exponent $\tau$ that remains consistent across different densities yet decreases as $U$ rises. At $U_c$, the exponent stabilizes at a specific value $\tau^*$, which aligns with the critical exponent derived from the saturation of entanglement entropy.

We introduce the problem of multi-target interactive search, where an agent seeks to locate multiple items within a metric space through interaction with an oracle. Unlike traditional single-target scenarios, this extension incorporates a finite budget of interactions, requiring the agent to gather sufficient information to locate all goals before exhausting their budget. We demonstrate that even with limited queries, meaningful information acquisition is possible, enabling agents to identify small neighborhoods around each multi-target. We establish theoretical bounds for both known and unknown multi-target locations, demonstrating a significant performance gap between these two cases. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm that achieves these theoretical limits when the target count is known and numerically match existing results for unknown single targets. Finally, we evaluate our approach in the context of nearest neighbor data structures, showing our methods outperform current state-of-the-art techniques in that specific domain.

Quantum machine learning holds promise for accelerating machine inference and training on both near-term and fault-tolerant quantum hardware. However, existing quantum classifiers are highly susceptible to noise, which can lead to erroneous predictions. This study introduces two novel classes of adversarial threats specific to quantum models: universal adversarial instances and universal adversarial perturbations. The former consists of input data that triggers label flips across every sample in the dataset, while the latter comprises vector perturbations capable of inducing classification errors for any input. The paper establishes the existence of universal perturbations for binary quantum classifiers and outlines specific conditions required for their existence in multi-class scenarios. Additionally, universal adversarial instances are analyzed within the context of quantum classifiers. Finally, a proof-of-concept demonstration evaluates the feasibility of creating universal adversarial instances using parameterized quantum circuits.

This work investigates the Steklov eigenvalues of planar domains that are nearly circular. We demonstrate that the first ten indices align with those of a disk, while the subsequent spectrum begins with a new branch. Furthermore, we derive the initial terms of the asymptotic expansion for these evolving eigenvalues as they depend on a specific Steklov parameter. We also compute the coefficients of said expansion for various scenarios. These findings are validated through a combination of analytical reasoning and numerical simulations.

We introduce a method for checking conformance between two sequences of infix or infix-like trace fragments, a problem that is NP-complete. We also describe how to construct the conformity graph for these fragment pairs and introduce a conformity script to manage them. We demonstrate that determining the emptiness of the fragment conformity language is an inherently difficult task. We further provide a formal definition of structural conformity for trace fragments and clarify that the proposed methods for infix fragment conformity are specifically designed to capture this structural relationship.

This study introduces a deep learning-based model designed to predict downlink radio signal strength at specific locations within cellular environments. We constructed a convolutional neural network (CNN) that accepts a two-dimensional grid representation of the network layout as input, utilizing cell tower coordinates and the directional orientation of sector antennas. The model's output corresponds to the received signal power across the grid points. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieves high accuracy in network prediction, performing better than conventional methods. Furthermore, we evaluated the model's utility in supporting drive test data validation and optimizing new deployments to enhance signal strength.

This paper introduces a straightforward temporal planning problem formulation and presents an algorithm to solve it, with both issues addressed through formal semantics. We then employ Isabelle/Haw to formally verify the proposed algorithm's correctness and conduct a practical implementation of this process.

This paper introduces a new metric designed to evaluate power system expansion models, offering a systematic method to calibrate model parameters. Specifically, it quantifies the degree to which an expansion model reflects the actual behavior of real-world power markets. The methodology is demonstrated using two modeling approaches—Capacity Expansion Models (CEMs) and Integrated Expansion Models (IEEs)—applied to the Western European market over a 20-year planning horizon.

Software maintenance relies heavily on effective code understanding, where identifying relevant concepts is a critical component of this process. While various techniques exist for locating these concepts, a persistent challenge remains in determining the optimal set of search keywords to support a maintenance task. This paper introduces a novel approach named STRICT (Search Keyword Identification via Information Theoretical methods) to automatically derive and refine search keywords from initial user inputs. By integrating information retrieval strategies with a iterative cycle of refinement and expansion, STRICT effectively enhances the relevance of keyword suggestions. Empirical results demonstrate that this iterative methodology surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in generating highly relevant keywords for code concept localization.

Colloidal gels are highly attractive for numerous applications due to their tunable mechanical and flow properties, yet their inherent yield stress often hinders processing. This study demonstrates that applying ultrasonic vibrations can effectively reduce the yield stress of colloidal gels, thereby facilitating handling and processing. We investigate the rheo-acoustic behavior of a thixotropic colloidal gel across a range of ultrasonic frequencies and amplitudes. Our findings reveal that, unlike typical thixotropic materials, the viscosity of this gel does not decrease under acoustic agitation. Instead, the observed gelation is driven by the formation of weak, short-lived clusters that break apart due to acoustic forces. Additionally, we demonstrate that colloidal gels can be treated as "rheo-acoustic" materials whose mechanical characteristics can be precisely adjusted through controlled acoustic manipulation.

This paper examines the Collatz Conjecture, a renowned unsolved problem in mathematics. The study analyzes the sequence's behavior, including its growth rate, frequency of occurrence, and relationship to other areas of mathematics, and explores the possibility of proving or disproving the conjecture through various approaches. The paper also investigates the implications of the conjecture's resolution for the broader mathematical community and highlights the importance of further research in this area.

Recent research has seen a surge in the application of machine learning to STEM document classification. While this trend is positive, it often relies on reusing existing labeled datasets without scrutinizing their annotation accuracy. This paper introduces a novel method for detecting labeling errors in STEM documents through Entity Linking in Mathematics (ELM). By applying this technique to the ScienceQA dataset, we identified numerous instances of incorrect labels. Our results demonstrate that ELL-based label error detection significantly enhances the performance of machine learning models on re-annotated data compared to those trained on the original, flawed labels.

This paper investigates proposal strategies within the context of stable matching, specifically analyzing how an agent's submitted preferences influence both their match and overall utility. We demonstrate that an agent can significantly enhance their outcome by strategically revealing only a subset of preferences rather than providing their entire ranking. We establish that an agent seeking to maximize their position should focus on proposing only those requests that result in a superior final match. Furthermore, we show that the set of proposals yielding the absolute best possible outcome is not necessarily a subset of those yielding the second-best outcome. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm capable of determining the optimal set of proposals for any given agent.

Summary extraction aims to generate a condensed version of a document that retains its core meaning. While numerous models have been created for this task, they are typically evaluated using existing standard metrics. However, these standard measures often exhibit high correlation with human judgments only under specific conditions, such as when gold-standard summaries are grammatically flawless and generated by humans within a controlled domain. Consequently, their reliability is compromised when dealing with machine-generated summaries or those from diverse fields. To address these limitations, we introduce SummScore, a novel, comprehensive assessment metric for summary quality. SumScore employs a cross-encoder architecture to compute the relevance between a source document and a given summary. Empirical results demonstrate that SummScore achieves a higher correlation with human ratings compared to traditional metrics. Furthermore, it outperforms existing approaches in both distinguishing between a human-written ideal summary and a machine-generated version, and in detecting domain-mismatched summaries.

This study addresses the challenge of recovering a signal $x^*$ residing in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ from limited data of the form $y_m = \langle x^*, b_m \rangle^2$ for $m=1, \dots, m$, where the vectors $b_m$ are drawn independently and identically (i.i.d.) according to a specific distribution. We demonstrate that when the number of measurements $m$ is sufficiently large, this framework enables the unique reconstruction of $x^*$. This result is significant because it reveals a unique solvability property inherent to quadratic measurements, a feature not shared by standard linear models. We establish a robust, stable, and computationally efficient algorithm grounded in semi-definite programming (SDP) to recover the signal. Furthermore, we prove that the number of measurements required for exact recovery is proportional to the intrinsic dimension of the target signal class. Empirical evaluations across various scenarios confirm the algorithm's performance, demonstrating that it achieves precise recovery with a count of measurements that is nearly optimal up to a constant factor.

We introduce BEVFusion, an end-to-end LiDAR-camera fusion framework that leverages a bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation to fuse sensor features. This approach utilizes a unified 2D feature space derived from LiDAR to align camera features, followed by a weighted summation to integrate them. BEVFusion offers a straightforward yet highly effective solution for multi-sensor fusion, achieving a significant reduction in model complexity and hyperparameter tuning requirements. When evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, BEVFusion achieves a 40.0 mAP and 22.8 AP for 3D object detection, as well as 36.3 WPE and 66.3 mAPH for trajectory prediction, all while relying on no more than 20% of the parameters found in state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the impact of temperature fluctuations on the dissipation regime of fluid turbulence. Theoretical analysis indicates that the spectral energy distribution remains unchanged by thermal effects, regardless of the strength of the temperature fluctuations. Theoretically, the spectral energy distribution is unaffected by temperature effects, regardless of the magnitude of temperature variations. Theoretical predictions are validated through direct numerical simulations of incompressible, periodic, three-dimensional flows with temperature as an additional variable. The simulations confirm that the spectral energy distribution is independent of temperature influences across a wide range of magnitudes. The numerical results align

This study presents a thorough numerical investigation of laser-induced temperature profiles within liquids to elucidate the complex diffraction patterns arising from the liquid's thermally induced, spatially varying refractive index. We demonstrate that the spatial distribution of the refractive index is governed by the cumulative temperature history at each point, necessitating a simulation that accounts for both the propagation of the electromagnetic field and the subsequent thermal evolution. We applied this methodology to analyze the diffraction patterns of a laser beam passing through a liquid layer heated by a second laser. We show that the resulting patterns are highly sensitive to the intensity distribution of the heating laser, as well as the specific thermophysical properties of the liquid. Furthermore, the patterns exhibit significant temporal evolution, a phenomenon attributed to the time-dependent nature of the thermal profile's development.

**Context:** Software design discussions typically occur within natural language formats across diverse channels, ranging from email threads to integrated tools. Extracting relevant design information from these unstructured textual sources is crucial for enhancing software quality.

**Objective:** This study introduces a novel approach to automatically extract design concepts from natural language extraction tasks.

**Methodology:** The investigation centers on the "stability" of these extraction results, evaluating how they hold up against variations in the underlying task definition.

**Findings:** The analysis reveals significant instability when definitions change, particularly concerning the stability of design classes.

**Implications:** These observations suggest a need for future research to develop Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques capable of producing more stable outcomes regardless of definitional shifts.

**Conclusion:** A deeper understanding of this instability is essential for refining software design knowledge mining efforts.

This work introduces H-STREAM, a novel system designed to manage vast volumes of streaming data alongside historical datasets. The system is engineered to support diverse data types, including streaming streams, continuous queries, batch processing, and historical queries. It achieves this by integrating three core components: the T-Engine, the T-Stream architecture, and the T-Stream Hist-Stream framework. The study details the system's architecture, its design choices, and the implementation of its core functionalities. Furthermore, the authors present an analysis of the system's performance and evaluate its capabilities in handling complex analytics pipelines. The results indicate that H-STREAM effectively and efficiently processes complex queries, demonstrating that it can manage demanding workloads with high throughput. The study concludes by highlighting the system's potential for real-world applications and identifying areas for future research.

In Randall-Sundrum models, the interaction between standard model particles and their heavy Kaluza-Klein partners generates resonant structures in parton-level distributions when these partners are produced directly. We present a novel class of non-resonant illustrations at both the top and bottom partner levels, designed to facilitate searches for these alternatives that do not rely on resonant signatures. We provide a unified analytical framework for these non-resonant effects, demonstrating that their intensity is governed by the degree of mass splitting between the spin-1/2 and spin-3/2 partners within the top or bottom sector.

Knowledge-based Neural Machine Translation (T) aims to leverage external knowledge bases to enhance translation capabilities. Knowledge-driven SPARQL machines are a specific subset of this field, designed to generate translations by querying knowledge bases. However, these systems face a significant limitation: they cannot process items in the input or output that lack corresponding entities in the knowledge base. To resolve this, we introduce a duplication mechanism that enables models to handle such cases effectively. Our approach demonstrates that incorporating this mechanism improves the overall quality of translations produced by the system.

Academic research relies on metrics to evaluate the impact of scholarly work, yet the current system is flawed. Researchers often prioritize publishing in venues with high average citation counts, which skews these metrics and benefits only a select group of established institutions. This creates a feedback loop that marginalizes others, fostering inequality and hindering the advancement of science. This paper introduces "Venue Analytics," a straightforward alternative to citation-based measures. By tracking publication counts over time rather than focusing on citation volumes, this method offers an equitable assessment of venue prestige. We validate "Venue Analytics" by applying it to computer vision research, demonstrating its ability to accurately reflect venue quality while also highlighting the inequities inherent in the traditional system.

This study presents a validation approach for control loop performance by employing a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the relationship between system inputs and outputs. The RNN is trained on operational data to approximate the closed-loop dynamics, which are subsequently analyzed using Bode and Nyquist diagrams. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a case study involving a liquid level control system.

This study introduces a functorial method for grouping elements into nested clusters with overlapping relationships, presenting a formal extension to the original functorial hierarchical grouping introduced by Kozak et al. in 2018, which was limited to non-overlapping structures. We demonstrate the utility of this concept by applying it to model structural variations in human genes, specifically deletions and duplications, as observed in tumor cells. These variations are detected through high-throughput sequencing and characterized as intervals along the genome. Our analysis utilizes a dataset of 20 human tumor samples containing 2,000 intervals each, with the goal of reconstructing the gene configuration of the underlying healthy cell. To achieve this, we define a probability measure over possible groupings and employ the normalizing constant associated with this measure to conduct Bayesian inference regarding the cell's gene structure.

Tensor Completion (TC) has emerged as a robust framework for recovering missing visual data, yet existing approaches often struggle with the high computational costs associated with non-streaming strategies. This paper introduces a new method, named PTLR, which leverages patch tracking to enable streaming Tensor Completion. PTLR transforms the global optimization problem into a series of efficient, localized subproblems. The proposed patch tracking strategy iteratively aligns similar local structures across different completion stages, allowing the global solution to be constructed incrementally. Furthermore, the tracking mechanism facilitates the rapid convergence of a new adaptive kernel function. Extensive experiments on tensor datasets with varying levels of missing information demonstrate that PTLR achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art streaming and non-streaming techniques.

The analysis focuses on determining the degree, grading, and Lyndon word generators for these algebras. The proof strategy relies on the geometric representation of these quasiparticle groups, combined with the utilization of both the Coxeter long elements and specific generators of the group of quasiparticle. We present numerical simulations of weakly nonlinear waves in two dimensions that exhibit a crossover from wave-dominated to energy-dominated regimes. In the wave regime, the energy spectrum follows the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum, while the energy-dominated regime displays a distinct power-law behavior. These findings align with weak turbulence theory predictions for both the wave and energy-dominated states. Notably, the crossover to wave turbulence is not instantaneous; rather, it occurs over an extended period during which a transient spectrum emerges. This transient spectrum is steeper than the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum, and its existence is corroborated by analytical calculations.

This paper examines the iterative graph normalization technique applied to finding independent sets in graphs with maximum weight. We establish that iterative normalization is equivalent to submodular flow and demonstrate that it converges in polynomial time within bipartite graphs. Additionally, we derive a new approximation bound for bipartite graphs with maximum weight independent sets and present a polynomial-time algorithm capable of achieving this approximation.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties of a gate-tuned, electrically responsive graphene layer at equilibrium, focusing on the impacts of an applied electric field. We demonstrate that a perpendicular electric field modulates the monolayer's thermodynamic behavior, causing a shift in the first-order phase transition temperature and introducing a second-order transition. Furthermore, we observe that entropy reduction and an enhanced out-of-plane susceptibility occur under electric field application, with a residual electric field effect persisting even after the return to an ungated state. Additionally, we note that a lateral electric field generates a novel mechanism for horizontal magnetoresistance.

The electron-cyclotron maser (EMC) mechanism is widely recognized as the most plausible explanation for the radio bursts generated by Jupiter's Io plasma torus and Saturn's Enceladus. This study reports the detection of radio emission from the flare star binary system CR Draconis, which is the closest known analog to the Jupiter-Io system. We observed the system using the UTR-2 radio telescope over a period of 100 days, covering a frequency range of 10.5 to 14.5 MHz. The data reveal a persistent, long-term emission lasting approximately 100 days, which is interrupted by significant flares. The emission spectrum spans 10.5 to 14.5 MHz, with a maximum rate of change (drift rate) of 1.5 MHz s$^{-1}$. The emission source is estimated to be located at a distance of 10$^{13}$ cm from the star, with a physical size of roughly 10$^{11}$ cm. These findings confirm that the radio emission originates near the electron cyclotron frequency of CR Draconis, supporting the hypothesis that the emission is cyclotron maser in nature.

Virtual humans are essential in various applications, including video games, social networking, and telepresence. Although many methods exist for modeling human shapes, they typically fail to account for individual body characteristics. This paper introduces Articulated Neural Representations (ANRs), an innovative technique designed to capture unique human features through a single, unified, and efficient neural field. Specifically, ANR utilizes a shared, lightweight, and efficient neural field capable of simulating articulated human motion. The approach combines principles of skeletal modeling and volumetric representations, utilizing a unified continuous parameter space to describe both skeletal poses and body cross-sections. By employing cross-sectional areas, the method effectively models shape variations caused by tissue, bone, and air. Furthermore, an efficient, learnable deformation field translates these neural fields to create diverse shapes and appearances. Experimental results demonstrate that our method is both highly efficient and effective.

Although human vision is inherently robust, it degrades under extreme image transformations in a manner distinct from computer vision algorithms. This study introduces a dataset comprising 1,000 images, each processed through 100 distinct transformations to create 100,000 samples. Utilizing this augmented dataset, we evaluate various computer vision techniques and conduct comparative analyses against human performance. Our findings reveal that while computers struggle significantly less than humans under these extreme conditions, specific transformations impact performance differently; for instance, humans are more susceptible to certain manipulations than machines. Furthermore, we identify that human susceptibility to severe transformations diminishes as the quantity of available training data increases. Ultimately, these results underscore the necessity of developing more resilient computer vision systems that mirror human resilience under stress.

We present a three-strong connection between three major concepts: the topological Chern-Simons theory used to compute link invariants, the integral kernel of the Askey-Wilson matrix, and the Kauffman polynomial. Specifically, this relationship reveals that the kernel acting on the matrix is equivalent to the transition amplitudes derived from Chern-Simons theory, which also correspond to the transition probabilities of a quantum walk occurring on a Cayley graph of the braid group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the eigenvalues of the matrix are associated with the singular links and the flat connections within Chern-Simons, while the eigenvectors represent the specific configurations of these links and flat connections.

We introduce a novel quantum Monte Carlo approach for simulating spin-1/2 frustrated magnets, specifically targeting systems where the coupling between trimer units is weak. Through testing on a 2D lattice, the method demonstrates significant efficiency gains over cluster techniques used for non-frustrated systems with weak couplings. Our implementation achieves a computational speedup of approximately a factor of 100. Applied to the frustrated kagome lattice, the algorithm exhibits marked performance improvements, reducing the cost of calculating the specific heat at low temperatures by roughly an additional order of magnitude compared to standard algorithms.

We examine the $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (nSSM) in light of the latest LHC data and constraints from dark matter searches. By analyzing the nSSM parameter space, we determine the viable regions for electroweak symmetry breaking that remain consistent with current experimental limits. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of achieving a strongly first-order electroweak phase transition within this framework. Our findings indicate that such a transition could generate a global signal detectable by the LHC, specifically manifesting as a resonance in the Higgsstrahlung process ($ZZ \rightarrow hh$) within the $s$-channel. Additionally, we assess the potential for observing the cosmic gravitational waves produced by this phase transition, highlighting its prospects for detection by the LISA mission.

We introduce "High-z Sudoku," a diagnostic tool designed to evaluate the reliability of redshift measurements for galaxies at high redshift derived from multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. By applying this method to a sample of 1000 galaxies with redshifts $z<1.5$ of verified accuracy, we established a benchmark for identifying High-z galaxies ($z>1.5$) through the specific combination of the $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit metric and the magnitude of the difference between the input and calculated redshifts. This methodology was then employed to analyze the redshift reliability of 100 candidate sub-millimeter galaxies (SMGs) with $z>1.5$ identified by the Herschel Atacama Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (HERITAGE) survey. Our results indicate that 90% of these targets possess robust redshifts, while 10% are identified as spurious. Notably, the most problematic cases are characterized by a lack of near-infrared data, highlighting the critical necessity of such observations for validating high-redshift claims.

We examine the low-energy dynamical properties of a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using both exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group methods. Our findings reveal that the distinctive three-peak structure of the spin-spin correlation function, previously identified in the dimer-gap model, persists even when the dimer gap is removed. We attribute these features to the existence of a "symmetry-broken" state, which emerges from the competition between the dimer gap and the gapless sector. Additionally, we propose that the central peak corresponds to a "symmetry-liquid" state. These findings offer new insights into the nature of the symmetry-broken and symmetry-liquid phases in spin-liquid systems.

We examine the $Z_3$-broken phase of $SU(3)-$Higgs theory utilizing lattice simulations, specifically investigating the shift associated with confinement and deconfinement. This phase transition is characterized by the presence of complex doublet states, which we analyze alongside the theory's spectrum. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these complex doublets, the $Z_3$-breaking sector, and the observed confinement-deconfinement shift.

The structural and magnetic characteristics of the newly synthesized binary intermetallic Cr$_2$Al were examined using X-ray and neutron diffraction, as well as magnetization measurements. The compound crystallizes in the Cr$_2$FeSi-type tetragonal structure (space group $P4nm$). Its magnetic order is characterized by an in-plane antiferromagnetic arrangement with a propagation vector of **k** = (0, 0, 0), where the magnetic moments are oriented parallel to the $a$ and $b$ crystallographic axes. This configuration arises from the exchange interactions between Cr atoms, which are dominated by the nearest-neighbor coupling ($J_1$) and the combined influence of the next-nearest- and third-nearest-neighbor couplings ($J_2$ and $J_3$).

This study evaluates a kinetic model featuring a velocity-dependent collision frequency to simulate rarefied gas flows with hard-sphere molecules. The model's performance was benchmarked against the full Boltzmann equation across a range of Knudsen numbers in both channel flow and Couette flow scenarios. Results indicate that while the traditional constant collision frequency version aligns well with the Boltzmann equation solution under high Knudsen number conditions, it deviates significantly at low numbers. Introducing the velocity-dependent collision frequency effectively captures the influence of intermolecular potentials on the constant-mean-free-path model, thereby restoring accuracy during low Knudsen number regimes.

This approach, termed "naturalized semantics," posits that an agent's existing functions can serve as interpreters for a language, thereby enabling the acquisition of semantic knowledge from minimal examples. We formalize this using the concepts of an agent's "theory" (its collection of interpreters) and "axioms" (the meanings assigned to symbols). We demonstrate that, given a suitably chosen theory, an agent can derive non-trivial semantics with virtually no prior training data. We further show that an agent's physical interaction with its environment provides valuable theoretical constraints. The future Electron-Proton Collider (EPC) arm of the project is designed to measure Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs) and Exclusive Vector Meson Production (EVMP) by precisely tracking scattered electrons. These measurements demand a detector capable of exceptional precision, high granularity, and robust performance under radiation. This paper reviews the current status of R&D efforts for the forward silicon trackers, detailing the results of sensor and wafer evaluations, bonding and dicing processes, and readout system development.

Astronomers have identified a low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) in the galaxy NGC 4395, which exhibits a luminosity of approximately $10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$. This object displays a complex light curve characterized by both short-term fluctuations and long-term variations. We propose that these features are best explained by turbulent accretion occurring within a radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF). In this scenario, short-term changes result from turbulence-induced fluctuations in the density and velocity of the inflow, while long-term trends reflect the AGN's average luminosity. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted numerical simulations of the RIAAF and analyzed synthetic light curves using the same analytical methods applied to the observational data. Our results indicate that an accretion rate of roughly $0.0001$ M$_{\odot}$/yr is required to reproduce the observed variability. Furthermore, we calculated the AGN's bolometric efficiency to be approximately 10% of the standard value, yielding a black hole mass of approximately $3 \times 10^5$ M$_{\odot}$.

This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260, a young Herbig Be star, utilizing the ESPaDOnS instrument on the CFHT. The data reveal a significant, previously unknown magnetic field component oriented radially outward from the stellar surface. This discovery was made possible by analyzing the polarization signatures within Hα and Hβ lines that originate from stellar wind material. The findings are consistent with a model where the magnetic field strength diminishes exponentially as it extends into the wind. Furthermore, the observed effects align with a scenario in which the magnetic field becomes negligible at a distance of approximately 10 stellar radii ($\sim 10 R_*$). The detection of this radial field component is attributed to the high sensitivity of emission lines to wind conditions, a capability that is further enhanced by Non-Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium (NLTE) effects.

We provide a probabilistic interpretation of the one-dimensional Dunkl intertwinement operator $J$ acting on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ using the free boson Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_b$. Within this framework, the polynomial $\varphi_n(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n!}} H_n(x) e^{2\alpha x}$ serves as an eigenfunction of $J$ with the eigenvalue $(-1)^n(1+2\alpha)^n$. This result yields the discrete orthogonality relation $\langle H_n, H_m \rangle_{d,\alpha} = (n+\alpha)^{\delta_{nm}}$, where the subscript denotes the Dunkl inner product associated with $\alpha$. Furthermore, by invoking the free boson Fock space $\mathcal{H}_F$ and the creation operator $a^\dagger$, we construct a generalized orthogonal basis $\Phi_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n!}} (a^\dagger)^n e^{x}$ for $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. The action of $J$ on $\Phi_n$ generates the orthogonal basis $\Psi_n(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n!+\alpha^n}} (a^\dagger)^n e^{(1+\alpha)x}$ for the space of polynomials under the Dunkl inner product.

We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the starburst galaxy NGC 5253, a system known for its low metallicity. The study covers the entire galaxy with a spatial resolution of 1.5 kpc, revealing a compact, bright core that is spatially aligned with the star-forming regions identified in the H$\alpha$ spectrum. By comparing the H30$\alpha$ data with existing H$\alpha$ measurements, we derived the stellar surface density map for NGC 5253. This analysis indicates that the star formation in the galaxy's core is driven by massive stars exceeding 100 solar masses, a finding consistent with the low metal environment. Additionally, we estimated the stellar age in the core to be less than 10 million years, suggesting a recent star formation event. These results demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tool for studying star formation in low-metallicity environments.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating the current state of an epidemic by developing an observer to reconstruct the process dynamics. The analysis focuses specifically on two distinct transmission mechanisms: the basic SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) and the simplified SI (Susceptible-Infected) epidemic models. For both frameworks, a novel observer structure is proposed, and its convergence properties are demonstrated. The practical application of the proposed method is illustrated through a case study involving the COVID-19 pandemic.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly employed to model intricate real-world entities and their relationships. While static KG models have achieved significant success in tasks like entity linking and link prediction, leveraging them for temporal KGs (T-KGs) remains an under-explored area. This paper addresses the challenge of performing link prediction on T-KG s by adapting static models. We introduce a novel strategy that transforms T-KG s into a set of static subgraphs, enabling the application of static models for predicting static links. Subsequently, we develop an algorithm to identify the most promising temporal relationships based on these static predictions. We further refine this process by incorporating a temporal consistency loss function to enhance the accuracy of our link prediction. Empirical evaluations on three prominent T-KG datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Ultrafast Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators are vital for both fundamental research and technological applications, yet they often operate in an unstable zone characterized by intense self-focusing and severe thermal effects. To address this, we present a geometric framework for analyzing the intracavity beam waist, incorporating both Kerr self-focusing and the absorption-induced thermal lens. This study also examines how the position of the laser crystals within the resonator impacts the resulting beam waist. We further explore the relationship between the beam waist and the cavity's confocal state, concluding that the cavity should be kept slightly below the confocal regime to achieve a stable, minimal waist. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations, which further demonstrate that the cavity geometry can be optimized to sustain a stable waist even in the presence of negligible or absent lensing.

We begin by establishing theoretical foundations for both online learning and federated learning within this context, demonstrating that the proposed strategy ensures an optimal convergence rate for both approaches while remaining adaptable to a broad spectrum of learners. This study introduces a novel back reflector design for silicon-on-insulator (SOI) photodetectors, utilizing silicon nanowire templates to create a 3D photonic band gap (PBG) structure. By tailoring the PBR's optical properties, the device achieves absorption enhancement in both thin and ultrathin active silicon layers. Experimental results show that for a 100 nm silicon film, the average absorption is enhanced by 1.5x, while a 50 nm film sees an enhancement of 1.2x, compared to a standard metal mirror. This absorption boost stems from the suppression of absorption in the long-wavelength spectral range. Furthermore, the photonic band gap back reflector maintains a low index of refraction outside the band gap, enabling efficient light trapping through total internal reflection.

This study examines the magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ (GICHO) using neutron scattering and magnetization measurements. The findings reveal a quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb honeycomb lattice, which orders antiferromagnetically at a critical temperature of $T_{\rm N} = 2.8$ K. The magnetic structure is characterized by a propagation vector of $\vec{k} = (0.5,0.5,0)$ and a non-collinear spin alignment. Specifically, spins within the honeycomb layers are ferromagnetically aligned along the $\vec{a}$-axis, while adjacent layers exhibit an antiferromagnetic coupling. The spin orientation within a single layer is rotated by $90^\circ$ relative to the crystallographic $\vec{c}$-axis. Furthermore, the magnetic phase diagram was constructed by analyzing the temperature and magnetic field dependencies of the order parameter.

Link prediction in sparse networks is a critical challenge with wide-ranging applications, from social media analysis to medical research. While recent research has focused on embedding-based methods for this task, existing approaches often fail to accurately capture the link prediction task in sparse networks. To address this, we introduce Sparse Structure Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel node representation technique designed to improve link prediction performance. SSNE captures the structural characteristics of sparse networks by utilizing the adjacency matrix and higher-order network structures derived from tensor factorization. By integrating these structural features, our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on link prediction tasks in sparse networks.

We introduce an atomic vapor cell fabricated using deep silicon micromachining techniques, featuring a 2 cm length and 1 cm² cross-section with internal microstructures to maximize surface area. These 3D internal designs facilitate efficient heat dissipation, allowing the cell to accommodate a large vapor volume at moderate temperatures. Our device was evaluated for use in atomic clocks and magnetometers, and its performance was benchmarked against a standard 1 cm-long flat-walled silicon vapor cell.

In contemporary optical communication, the adoption of dual-polarization four-dimensional (DP4D) modulation formats has become prevalent. These formats leverage amplitude, phase, and both polarization states to transmit data, offering superior spectral efficiency and robustness against fiber impairments. However, as signal power intensifies to maximize transmission distance, nonlinear effects emerge, distorting the received signal. This distortion is most pronounced in power, which undergoes nonlinear fluctuations that degrade the performance of nonlinearly filtered DP4D modulation formats. This study introduces a comprehensive model for nonlinear disturbance power across various DP4D formats. The model accounts for the influence of nonlinear phase noise on amplitude, cross-phase modulation (XPM), and self-phase modulation (SPM). By analyzing the power dynamics of the in-phase and quadrature components of the complex field, the research reveals that nonlinear distortions in amplitude are primarily driven by cross-phase noise acting on the in-phase component. Furthermore, the model incorporates the impact of polarization-dependent nonlinearities, which cause asymmetry in distortion between the two polarization arms. Validation against split-step Fourier method (SSFM) simulations confirms the accuracy of this analytical approach.

Integrating visible and infrared imagery is a viable strategy to enhance image quality for smoke detection in wild fires. This paper introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel integration framework built upon Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that utilizes visible images as a prior to reconstruct missing data regions in incomplete infrared images. FIRe-GAN employs a dual-structure design featuring a generator and an auxiliary discriminator. The primary discriminator distinguishes between real visible images and those synthetically generated by the network, while the secondary auxiliary discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the fused visible-infrared outputs. The training process is guided by a composite loss function combining adversarial losses from both discriminators with an $L_1$ reconstruction loss. Evaluated against three established fusion benchmarks, FIRe-GAN demonstrates superior performance in fidelity, contrast, and structural preservation. Furthermore, its effectiveness in smoke detection tasks is validated through comparison with existing integration methods.

This study introduces a novel dataset designed to identify indicators of depression in social media content. We outline the dataset creation process, offering an in-depth empirical analysis of its characteristics and a comparative evaluation of various machine learning models for detecting depressive signs. Results indicate that a Random Forest classifier trained on the proposed dataset achieves a 72% accuracy rate.

COVID-19 emerged in late 2019 in Wuhan, China, and has since evolved into a global pandemic. This study introduces a novel stochastic compartmental model for the disease, characterized by random transitions between all defined compartments. The paper examines the model's fundamental properties, including moment dynamics, a unique equilibrium, and the behavior of its stationary distribution. Additionally, it establishes the model's positive ergodicity and provides numerical simulations to support these findings.

This study investigates the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, specifically examining the impact of coupling between the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole components. Using the Quasiparticle Random Phase Approximation (QRPA), we demonstrate that this coupling significantly influences the ISGMR centroid energy, causing a substantial red shift. These findings align with the results from the Finite-Range Relativistic Hartree-Bock (FRRHB) calculations.

This study examines the behavior of stick-slip dynamics in feedback-regulated systems exhibiting discontinuous Coulomb friction. We demonstrate that the system's convergence properties are invariant regardless of whether it begins in a sticking or slipping state. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a Convergence Set, which accounts for all potential convergences to the Constrained Equilibrium Set (ES). This allows the system to reach a Constrained Equilibrium Set (ES) in a finite timeframe. Additionally, we prove that all other ES points are unstable. Finally, we establish that the boundary of the Convergence Set coincides with the boundary of the region of attraction associated with the Constrained Equilibrium Set (ES).

This study introduces a novel approach to optimizing reinsurance strategies within a compound Poisson framework by employing deep learning techniques. Specifically, we utilize a compound neural network designed to generate an approximate value function that satisfies the discretized deep Bellman equation. This method enables the determination of deep Bellman-optimal reinsurance policies. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our proposed approach yields policy structures that are both intuitive and superior in performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Sequential models are widely used to predict the next item in a user's sequence, primarily by counting the appearances of each item and calculating transition probabilities between them. This study introduces a model that explicitly accounts for the fact that users interact with systems in multiple contexts, utilizing purpose-based modeling to represent these contexts as latent factors. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the model's performance. Furthermore, the revealed latent purposes offer actionable insights for enhancing user experiences.

This paper examines the double-confluent Heun equation (DCHE) in a specific limit where one integral constant diverges, a case for which no standard DCDC solution exists. We demonstrate that a valid family of solutions can be constructed by taking the limit of the three regular DCHe solutions, each characterized by distinct angular momentum values. Furthermore, we establish that this DCHe form represents a particular symmetric unfolding of the source term in Heun's equation, achieved by introducing an infinite array of singularities that tend toward the origin. Finally, we confirm that the resulting reducible DCHe equation is a special instance of the infinite-symmetry Heun equation, which is equivalent to the infinite-product of SL(2,R) Heun polynomials.

This work examines the estimation of a rank-one matrix under groupwise heteroskedasticity, where the column-wise heterogeneity is modeled via a vector of positive, unknown variances. This framework encompasses significant applications such as portfolio optimization, network analysis, and high-dimensional statistics. By establishing the minimax rates for estimating both the matrix and its latent vector, we demonstrate that the performance limits hinge on the heterogeneity of these variances. Specifically, when variances are partitioned into a constant finite number of balanced groups, the fundamental bounds mirror those of the homoskedastic scenario. Conversely, if group sizes are unbalanced, the bounds adaptively reflect the achieved efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce an estimator that matches these optimal lower bounds, achieving optimality up to a logarithmic factor.

While numerous theoretical frameworks describe topological phases without symmetries, the recent consensus holds that intrinsic topology in non-symmetric systems requires fine-tuning, which undermines the stability essential for such states. In this study, we introduce a comprehensive topological model lacking any symmetries and devoid of fine-tuning, demonstrating that the necessary ingredients for intrinsic topology are surprisingly minimal. We establish that the system's band structure is defined by a two-dimensional non-Hermitian generalization of the Dirac equation, which accounts for the diverse topological behaviors observed. Furthermore, we illustrate the physical manifestations of these intrinsic topological properties through the system's bulk-boundary correspondence and its characteristic skin effect.

The lepton flavor-mixed process $B\to X_b\ell^+\ell^-$ is examined using the ratio $\mathcal R$, which compares the inclusive $b\to s\tau^+\tau^-$ channel against the inclusive $b\to s\ell^+\tau^-$ one. This ratio is calculated within the framework of the Operator Product Expansion (OPE), with a focus on the low-$q^2$ domain. Our findings indicate that the $\mathcal R$ value in the region $q^2<8\text{ GeV}^2$ is approximately 0.15, with an uncertainty of roughly 10%. This level of precision is deemed sufficient to detect the lepton flavor universality violation observed in the $B_s$ decay channel, specifically the $\tau$ anomaly.

This study addresses the design of decentralized control for linear time-invariant multi-input multi-output systems, focusing on achieving performance that remains non-interfering among subsystems. The core approach involves partitioning the system into independent units, each governed by a local controller that manages only its assigned channel without interaction from others. The research establishes both necessary and sufficient criteria for the existence of such controllers to meet a defined set of non-interference metrics. Furthermore, the work introduces a distributed algorithm enabling robust, decentralized system management for configurations that are already operating effectively. This plug-and-play scheme ensures that when a subsystem is added or removed, the global system stabilizes autonomously through local adjustments, requiring no centralized coordination.

In the initial phase, text is encoded into BERT vectors, which are then fed into a classifier to predict the disease category. The subsequent phase involves training a new classifier on updated BERT representations specifically tailored to enhance performance. Research on social and other networks has expanded rapidly in recent years, driven by the growing availability of data and computational resources. This surge has created a pressing need for a comprehensive guide tailored to network scientists who may not be experts in every aspect of field. The authors present "The Atlas for the Ambitious Network Scientist," designed to fill this gap. This work offers a thorough overview of the field's core concepts, methods, and techniques, while also addressing advanced topics such as modeling, statistical analysis, and visualizing networks. By doing so, it aims to serve as both a reference and a springboard for further exploration, supporting scholars in advancing their research within network science.

The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics focuses on the reciprocal interactions between ecological and evolutionary processes within systems. While the foundational concept dates back to the 19th century, it gained significant prominence in the 1970s and 1980s, particularly through the work of theodosius Dobzhansky and the development of quantitative frameworks. Despite this progress, establishing a unified theory remains elusive due to the intricate nature of these interactions. Consequently, research has branched into distinct areas: contemporary studies examine immediate feedback loops, whereas deep historical inquiries investigate the legacy of events stretching over millennia. This review analyzes the theoretical and empirical evidence supporting both contemporary and deep historical eco-evolutionary dynamics, highlighting the critical role of time delays and variable timescales. It further explores how contemporary rate modulators—such as environmental shifts, phenotypic plasticity, and demographic stochasticity—can amplify or dampen these effects across varying temporal scales. Additionally, the review addresses challenges in modeling and detecting these patterns through data analysis, ultimately aiming to synthesize current knowledge and outline a path toward a cohesive theory of eco-evolutionary dynamics.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become a primary method for speech representation extraction, demonstrating robustness across various tasks even with limited labeled data. However, the impact of SSL-derived adversarial examples on speech recognition remains largely unexamined. This study investigates the vulnerability of such attacks within the realm of spoken language understanding. We evaluate the Susceptibility of Speech Self-supervised Learning (S2SL), comparing it against traditional methods like Mel-frequency cepstrual coefficients (MFCC) and analyzing the relationship between dataset size and attack performance. Our findings indicate that S2SL is significantly more susceptible than MFCC and that adversarial examples degrade more severely as training datasets expand. Furthermore, we introduce a novel mitigation strategy that utilizes a white-box model to synthesize clean samples, which empirically reduces attack success rates.

This study examines the adoption of decentralized blockchain exchanges, utilizing the Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations framework to develop a model that predicts user adoption rates. The proposed model is trained on historical data from traditional centralized exchanges and applied to forecast the growth of decentralized platforms. This paper presents a sensitivity analysis approach for missing data problems within a Bayesian framework. It introduces a sensitivity parameter that varies between missing data mechanisms, specifically the E-value, a novel concept for this application. The method demonstrates that E-values can be utilized to generate posterior distributions for missing data, which in turn allows for the construction of posterior distributions for missing data mechanisms. The approach is applicable to diverse missing data contexts, including missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and selection bias, as well as untestable assumptions. The method's efficacy is illustrated through its application to a study examining the association between maternal smoking during pregnancy and low birth weight.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has created a demand for distributed learning architectures that leverage the expansive network of intelligent vehicles (IVs) to gather data. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for this purpose, enabling data analysis across vehicles without compromising privacy. Simultaneously, blockchain technology offers robust security and trust mechanisms that are increasingly vital for IoVs applications. This paper presents a systematic review of blockchain-enhanced FL frameworks specifically for the IoVs domain. Conducted through a comprehensive literature search, this study examines existing FL methods, the capabilities of blockchain, and the synergistic integration of both technologies within various scenarios. The findings reveal that while numerous FL studies exist, only a limited number of works address the specific intersection of FL, blockchain, and intelligent vehicle data. Consequently, this study offers significant insights for researchers and highlights critical research gaps and future directions, ultimately serving as a foundational guide for developing secure, privacy-preserving learning models within the evolving ecosystem of intelligent vehicles.

This study presents a measurement of beauty and charm quark production in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing non-prompt D mesons as a specific channel. The non-prompt component is isolated by identifying the D meson decay products originating from the decay of polarized $\Upsilon$ resonances. The measurement covers transverse momenta ($p_{\rm T}$) ranging from 1 to 30 GeV/$c$ and pseudorapidities between -0.3 and 2.4. Results for both the non-prompt and prompt contributions to the D-meson spectrum are provided, with the prompt section serving as a cross-check against existing data from the LHCb collaboration. The non-prompt results are compared with predictions from Monte Carlo simulations, which show reasonable agreement. Furthermore, this study offers a significant improvement in statistical precision over previous measurements of non-prompt D-mesons in proton-proton collisions.

The Fermilab Quantum Computing Facility is being developed to serve as a centralized environment for quantum computing research, accommodating up to 100 quantum processors cooled via a large-scale millikelvin dilution refrigerator. This facility is designed to foster collaborative efforts across experimental, theoretical, and computational domains, ultimately advancing our understanding of fundamental physics. This report outlines the project's objectives, current status, and future roadmap.

This study examines 100 cases of crypto misuse across software systems, including 25 instances for each of authentication, encryption, key management, and key exchange. The research highlights that developers frequently rely on established libraries and standard practices, yet their implementations often contain significant flaws. These crypto abuses can result in severe repercussions, such as data breaches, unauthorized access, and denial of service. Consequently, there is an urgent need to raise developer proficiency in cryptography and to encourage the adoption of secure, standardized solutions.

We introduce a new automatic tagging framework designed for large-scale urban environments, which are characterized by an extensive variety of scene content and limited annotation labels. Our approach employs a voting-based strategy to determine the most probable object category for any given region. To ensure robustness, we utilize a powerful pre-trained network to generate features that encompass diverse visual information. These features are then mapped into a discrete set of visual words to facilitate voting-based classification. We evaluate our method on the SUN dataset, a large-scale database containing nearly 100,000 images across 376 categories. Our results demonstrate that the method achieves high accuracy even with sparse training data, reaching 92.2% average precision. Furthermore, we validate the approach on the newly introduced Cityvues dataset, which features 50 categories and nearly 100,000 images. On this challenging benchmark, our method attains an average precision of 70.2%.

This study introduces a novel nonconvex optimization network designed to solve lq-minimization problems, which are widely used for signal and image recovery. By adapting the proximal average method, the proposed approach, called NuSPAN, achieves accelerated convergence compared to current state-of-theart proximal algorithms. The method relies on a fixed-point iteration that converges to the unique fixed-point under mild conditions, with the convergence rate proven to match that of standard methods for sparsity promotion. The lq-norm's flexibility allows it to approximate both the l1- and l0-norms, making NuSPAN particularly effective for signal and image reconstruction tasks. The algorithm has been implemented for seismic reflectivity inversion, where the l1-norm promotes smoothness and the l0-norm encourages sparsity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network surpasses existing state-of-theart methods in terms of both computational efficiency and convergence speed.

This paper examines the indexical semigroups of composition operators on spaces comprising analytic functions on the open unit disk that possess finite growth conditions at the boundary. We derive a characterization for the strong continuity of these operator semigroups and establish a strong continuity condition for the associated integral operator semigroups under specific finite growth conditions on analytic functions. A significant result demonstrates that any weakly continuous semigroup of composition operators on these spaces that exhibits finite growth conditions at the boundary, is indeed strongly continuous.

This work investigates the finite-size scaling of the overlap between ground states in two critical 1D quantum spin chains, specifically focusing on how these overlaps behave when the systems differ by a single site. We demonstrate that such overlaps, in the limit of large lattice size, approach a constant value multiplied by a decaying term characterized by the minimal bulk conformal dimension. While the leading-order correction to the overlap follows a power law dictated by this minimal dimension, subleading corrections arise from the next excitations in the conformal dimension spectrum. We validate these predictions numerically for the Haagerup model, confirming the existence of the predicted universal amplitudes. Furthermore, we establish a connection between operator fusion in the theory and the structure of ground state intersections, providing an alternative framework for calculating operator fusion rules.

This study introduces a novel set-valued part-of-the-speech (SetPOS) tagging approach that simultaneously predicts a set of candidate tags along with their associated confidence scores for each candidate. By explicitly modeling uncertainty, this framework addresses the inherent ambiguity in morphosyntactic analysis. The resulting predicted distribution is converted into a set of high-confidence tags, which are then used to derive the final setPOS annotations. The research evaluates the performance of this setPOS DNN model and demonstrates that it outperforms a comparable single-best DNN in dependency parsing applications by relying on historical German texts.
